Subject: 'Warm Clay', a craft resource from the Workshop of Forms. A single fist-sized lump of freshly kneaded clay, warm ochre-terracotta, with deep finger and palm prints, moist and soft; a faint warmth seems to live inside its folds, as if it were still warm from the hands that knead it every day (subtle warmth, NOT lava, NOT fire). It rests on a worn wooden worktable dusted with pale sand, a small wooden spatula beside it. Background: the dim, silent, abandoned Workshop of Forms deep underground — a thin stream of sand falls from a crack in the dark vault like an hourglass that nobody turns; white-green crystals glow coldly from within in cracks of the stone wall; the shape of an unfinished clay hand lies on a shelf in the gloom. The whole hall is cold white-green; the clay is the only warm thing in it.

Subject: the floor of the Workshop of Forms, the first hall under the city of Endalor, where a god once sculpted living beings from clay and abandoned the work halfway. Large worn stone floor slabs with cracks; drifts and still ripples of pale sand. White-green crystals glowing from within grow only in the cracks along the edges and in the corners; their cold light spills onto the floor. In the corners: thin streams of sand fall from the unseen vault into small round piles with a faint haze, like hourglasses nobody turns. Along the left and right edges: parts of heavy wooden worktables seen from above with unfinished clay works lying on them — a hand without fingers, a face without features, half of a small beast — sculpting chisels, clay-stained cloths, clay pots. At the very top and bottom edges: the foot of the stone walls with half-formed clay bodies emerging from the stone, made precisely and calmly, unfinished, not grotesque. The hall is cold: near-black stone, white-green crystal light, pale sand. The only warm color is the ochre clay of the unfinished works. No candles, no fire, no warm lamps, no grid, no characters.

Промт, как он ушёл в модель
Art style: hand-painted stylized dark-fantasy game art for a mobile RPG. Painterly digital illustration with visible, confident brush strokes and simplified planar shapes, crisp rim light on edges, strong readable silhouettes, deep near-black shadows. Light tells the story: a few strong sources — crystals and cracks that glow from within — throw colored light upward, the light comes from below. Dust motes and grains of sand float in the light. Moderate detail, clean readable forms. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime. Match the brushwork, lighting and color handling of the attached style reference images: the first shows how we paint characters, the second shows the Workshop's clay and its cold white-green crystal light. Do NOT copy their subjects or composition.

Format: vertical enemy card portrait, 4:5, shown small on the battle field (about 74 px wide) and large in the bestiary. Three-quarter view, the figure fills most of the frame, head and shoulders in the upper third, clear readable silhouette. This is a NEW ORIGINAL design made from the description only. World rule: every creature of the Workshop of Forms was sculpted of clay by a god and left unfinished — the 'samples' are rough unfinished tries, each named after its missing or unfinished part; the 'servants' are more finished, with even hands, faces, aprons and tools; the Master is the only finished one, smooth and polished. Everything is made precisely and calmly — unfinished, but not ugly and not grotesque. Clay colors: grey-green and warm ochre, visible finger marks and tool strokes on the clay. Figures have elven proportions unless the description says otherwise. Background: the dim abandoned Workshop of Forms deep underground — dark stone, a thin stream of sand falling from a crack above, white-green crystals glowing from within in the cracks; darker and softer than the figure. The whole scene is lit by cold white-green crystal light from below; no red, orange or warm light; the clay is the only warm color. All fourteen creatures of this set share the same painting style, palette and lighting.

Subject: 'Faceless Sample', the first creature anyone meets in the Workshop. An elven figure of grey-green clay in a rough sketch of clothing, with a rope instead of a belt, holding a stone blank of a sword that has no crossguard yet. No face at all — only two shallow dents pressed by a thumb where the eyes should be; still it looks straight at the viewer. Made simply but solidly, honest, walks straight at you.

No text, no letters, no numbers, no runes that look like letters, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no UI elements, no border or frame around the picture. No gore, no blood, no horror grotesque.

World rule: every creature of the Workshop of Forms was sculpted of clay by a god and left unfinished — the 'samples' are rough unfinished tries, the 'servants' are more finished, with even hands, faces, aprons and tools, the Master is the only finished one. Everything is made precisely and calmly — unfinished, but not ugly and not grotesque. Every creature is made entirely of clay: a matte clay surface with finger marks, seams and tool strokes; no human skin, no realistic flesh; hair is sculpted clay; eyes are pressed hollows or smooth clay without pupils. They must not look like living people, orcs or goblins. Clay colors: grey-green and warm ochre. Background: the dim abandoned Workshop of Forms — dark stone, a thin stream of sand falling from above, white-green crystals glowing from within in the cracks; darker and softer than the figure. Lit by cold white-green crystal light from below; no red, orange or warm light; the clay is the only warm color. All fourteen portraits share the same framing, painting style, palette and lighting.

Subject: 'Hollow Sample', a shell. Its chest is open like an empty mould from which the casting was removed; nothing inside but wind. Head thrown back, thin arms spread, a whirl of sand and air bursting from its empty chest and mouth.

Painterly dark-fantasy card art, like a hand-painted oil sketch: visible textured brush strokes, simplified planar shapes, muted earthy colors, deep black shadows, crisp cold rim light, warm light from below, dust and sand hanging in the light. Enemy card portrait, 4:5. Camera at chest height. The creature is centered; the bottom edge of the picture cuts the body at the waist: head, torso and arms in frame, no hips, no legs — the legs are never visible, whatever the pose. The head sits in the upper third with a little space above it. It is an enemy: dangerous, alive and caught in action — not a specimen standing still like an exhibit. Its story reads from its body, its pose and the place around it. Every creature here is unfinished work of clay left by the god Vial in his Workshop of Forms; what is unfinished gives it its name and is clearly visible.

The creature: the One-armed Sample — a rare, fast assassin of the Workshop, an unfinished elf sculpted from grey-green clay in a hurry. It is alive and moving — not a statue, not a bust on a stand. Elven proportions, long pointed ears swept back, a fine sharp elven face with high cheekbones, narrow almond eyes and a thin hard mouth; long hair roughed in with a few fast strokes of clay. A sketch of a hunter's clothing: a strap across the chest and a scrap of clay cloth. The haste shows everywhere: thumb smears, unsmoothed seams, rough lumps of clay left on the body. Its single arm has no hand: the forearm narrows and continues straight into a long jagged blade of pale stone, in line with the arm, like a splinter chipped off a rock; the blade is the end of the arm. There is no hand, no fist and no fingers anywhere in the picture. On the other side of the body there is no shoulder and no arm: a clean, smooth, flat slope of clay runs from the neck down to the waist, as if an arm there was never planned. Pose: caught mid-lunge straight toward the viewer — the upper body thrown forward and low, head forward, facing the viewer so that both sides of the body are clearly visible: the blade arm swept back and low to one side, ready to slash upward, and the smooth empty slope on the other side. Hair and the scrap of cloth whip back, sand and dust are torn up around it. Gaze: cold, narrowed eyes slide past the viewer, fixed on someone behind — the healer in the back row. Background: the corner of the Workshop where it was made, dark and cold: a sculptor's workbench with a split stone block, a long splinter missing from it; stone chips and an abandoned mallet on the bench; a thin column of sand pouring from the dark vault; cold white-green crystals glowing in the cracks of the floor light it from below — the crystals are white-green, never orange or amber.

Background: its own place — a silent empty hall of the Workshop; open empty moulds of clay lie on the shelves and tables behind it, the same shape as its chest; a column of falling sand is torn and bent by its wind. Art style: hand-painted stylized dark-fantasy game art for a mobile RPG. Painterly digital illustration with visible, confident brush strokes and simplified planar shapes, crisp rim light on edges, strong readable silhouettes, deep near-black shadows. Light tells the story: a few strong sources — cracks and jade inlays in old stone that glow from within — throw colored light upward, the light comes from below. Cold and warm light contrast. Dust motes, pollen and tiny sparks float in the light. Moderate detail, clean readable forms. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime, no cartoon.

Format: wide horizontal battle background for a landscape phone screen, 21:9. Strict top-down orthographic view, the camera looks straight down at the ground like a tabletop RPG battle map: no horizon, no perspective, no side view of buildings, no sky. The attached image is our battle arena of a different place, the Workshop of Forms: take from it ONLY the straight-down camera, the scale, the layout of the zones and the painting style. Do NOT copy its objects, materials or colors: no worktables, no clay figures, no crystals, no sand. The game puts its cards along the left and right sides: five hero cards in the left quarter and five enemy cards in the right quarter, from the top edge to the bottom edge. So the left quarter (0-25% of the width) and the right quarter (75-100% of the width) must be open, flat, evenly lit ground over their whole height: plaza slabs, moss in the seams and fine cracks only — no steps, no walls, no statues, no bowls, no plants, no objects there. Unlike our biome arenas, this arena is a single scene: the fight begins and ends here, the camera never moves on to a next room, so nothing in the picture leads onward — no doorway, no road, no stairway, no passage out of the picture. The forest appears only as a thin dark strip along the very top and bottom edges, no more than 7% of the height. All details are placed only in the central half (25-75% of the width), close to the top and bottom edges; the middle of the central half stays calm and open, because the game shows banners there.

Subject: the great plaza of Ish-Kantun at night, at the foot of a jade stepped pyramid deep in an ancient forest, seen straight from above — the one place where the whole fight happens. It is night and the plaza is dark, as dark as our Workshop arena: the slabs are dark grey-green stone in deep shadow, and the light comes only from below — from glowing cracks and grooves and from the copal embers. Ground: large worn, tightly fitted stone slabs, some lifted and cracked by roots; dark moss in the seams, a few fallen leaves and scattered green feathers; thin cracks glow from within with cold jade-green light. In the central half only: along the top edge, the lowest tiers of a dark jade-green stepped pyramid seen straight from above — straight parallel step edges, cut off by the top edge of the picture; along the bottom edge, a great round stone calendar disc set flat into the plaza, seen straight from above, only its upper half visible, carved with a few broad concentric rings of large simple ornament — notches, spirals, feathers, jaguar spots; no small signs, no glyphs — with jade-green light glowing in its grooves; near the pyramid and near the disc, two wide stone bowls of smoldering copal resin with warm amber embers and thin curls of pale smoke; a few black obsidian shards and jade beads on the slabs. Along the very top and bottom edges runs a thin strip of dark forest leaves and roots; no big leaves in the corners, the left and right quarters stay clear. Near-black shadows, cold jade-green light; the only warm color is the amber glow of the copal embers. No characters, no animals, no bodies, no cards, no grid.

Enemy card portrait, 4:5, shown small on the battle field (about 74 px wide) and large in the bestiary. Camera at chest height, waist-up: the bottom edge of the picture cuts the body at the waist — head, torso and arms in frame, no hips, no legs; the legs are never visible, whatever the pose. The figure is centered and fills most of the frame; the head sits in the upper third with a little space above it. The body is turned in a three-quarter view toward the LEFT side of the picture, where its enemies stand; its weapon, its spell or the thing it is named after is thrust toward the left and clearly shown in front of the body. It is an enemy: dangerous, alive and caught in action — not a model posing, not a statue. Its story reads from its body, its pose and the place around it. World: these are the people of Ish-Kantun, an ancient, long-lived forest civilization of elves: jade stepped pyramids in a dark forest, cloaks and headdresses of feathers, obsidian blades, quilted cotton armor, jaguar pelts, great carved stone calendars; they counted their days in the circles of the Great Count, and when the circle ended they came out of the forest to take other people's breath and start the count anew. Their look is inspired by the ancient Maya, but they are clearly ELVES: tall and slender, long pointed ears, ageless narrow faces, warm bronze skin with dark painted patterns, heavy jade ear spools; they must not look like real-world people, orcs or goblins. Colors: muted and earthy, like all our enemies — deep jade green, dark bronze, bone white, obsidian black, dull old gold, a little faded red; everything else sinks into near-black shadow. Light, the same for the whole set: night; the light comes from below — cold jade-green light glowing from within cracks and jade inlays in old stone rises onto the figure; crisp cold rim light on its edges; a small warm amber glow of embers is the only warm light. Background: its own place in Ish-Kantun, darker and softer than the figure, with depth. All fifteen portraits of this set share the same framing, painting style, palette and lighting.

The enemy: the Feathered Archer, a rank-and-file archer of Ish-Kantun. A lean young elf with long pointed ears, long black hair tied up with bunches of dark green and grey feathers, a stripe of dark green paint across his eyes, a simple cotton wrap and a collar of bone beads; on his back a quiver of arrows fletched with the same feathers, and more feathers hang from the quiver. Action: he shoots from the foliage where no one can see him — half-hidden among giant dark leaves, only his face, arms and bow come out of them; he draws a long bow to full draw and aims to the left, the arrowhead a black obsidian point; his narrowed eyes are fixed on a target to the left. A breath of wind (Air) stirs the feathers and the leaves around him. Background: the dense night canopy of the forest of Ish-Kantun, huge leaves and hanging lianas; far below behind him, the dim shape of a stepped pyramid with a jade-green glow at its base.

Промт, как он ушёл в модель
Art style: hand-painted stylized dark-fantasy game art for a mobile RPG. Painterly digital illustration with visible, confident brush strokes and simplified planar shapes, crisp rim light on edges, strong readable silhouettes, deep near-black shadows. Light tells the story: a few strong sources — crystals and cracks that glow from within — throw colored light upward, the light comes from below. Cold and warm light contrast. Dust motes and grains of sand float in the light. Moderate detail, clean readable forms. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime. Match the brushwork, lighting and color handling of the attached style reference images, but do NOT copy their subjects, objects, letters or composition.

Format: vertical hero card portrait, 4:5. Half-body portrait from the waist or hips up, three-quarter view; no knees, no legs, no feet in the frame. The hero's body is turned toward the right side of the picture, toward unseen enemies beyond the right edge, and the face is seen in three-quarter view looking to the right. Head in the upper third, the face large, well lit and readable at small size; the lower quarter may be darker because the card puts the name there. Rich atmospheric background that tells where the hero lived, with depth and soft focus, darker than the character. Light comes from below and from glowing crystals; rim light separates the figure from the background.

Subject: Torbin the Sack, a dwarf tank of the Earth school; for thirty years he carried sacks of empty karst stone down the mountain road to an elven outpost and never took a single stone too many, and later he walked the roads beside a wandering elven healer, guarding her companions as if it were a fair deal. A stocky, broad-shouldered dwarf in his fifties with a sun-browned, honest face, a thick chestnut-brown beard tied with a leather cord, bushy brows, calm dependable eyes. A dusty travel jerkin of thick leather over a padded shirt, leather straps across the chest. Over his right shoulder he carries a heavy canvas sack; through its open neck show dull matte grey-white stones that do not glow at all. World: the Underground Forest, the finished creation of the god Vial deep under the city of Endalor — what his Workshop of Forms left half-done is finished here. Its hunters are finished elves: tall and lean, long pointed ears, fine narrow faces, both hands, clothes of woven bast and bark strips; their skin is pale as the trunks, smooth and matte like fine dense clay — they are the god's finished work, not living people, calm and unhurried. Its beasts are bigger than the beasts of the surface and move in packs. Colors: muted and cold, like all our enemies — bone-white bark, pale grey-green moss, dark bottle green, ash grey, a little honey-tan bast and dull ochre; everything else sinks into near-black shadow. Light, the same for the whole set: the light comes from below — cold white-green light glowing from within veins of crystal in the earth, pale roots and fallen leaves rises onto the figure and lights it from underneath; crisp cold white-green rim light on its edges; the only warm colors are the honey-tan of bast and a dull ochre. Background: its own place in the Underground Forest, darker and softer than the figure, with depth. All fourteen portraits of this set share the same framing, painting style, palette and lighting.

Background: a tangle of huge pale roots in the dark forest, glowing leaves on the ground, white-green light rising from a crack in the earth below him.

They wore sun discs of beaten gold, collars of obsidian and gold, crests of feathers made of flame; feathered fire serpents flew over their cities, and dogs of smoldering coal guarded them. Their look is inspired by the ancient Aztecs, but they are clearly SAGANS, not people: their bodies are living fire held in a human-like shape — a skin like a dark crust of cooling charcoal and obsidian, cracked all over, with orange-gold fire glowing through every crack; hair and beards of flame; eyes of white-gold fire; no human skin, no ordinary hair, no horns, no tails. No jade, no jungle, no stepped pyramids: their world is black glass, ash and fire. Colors: muted and smoky, like all our enemies — obsidian black, charcoal grey, ash white, dull old gold, deep ember red and orange; everything else sinks into near-black shadow. Light, the same for the whole set: night; the light comes from below — hot orange-red light of living fire glowing from within cracks in black obsidian and basalt, and from their own bodies, rises onto the figure; crisp cold pale-blue reflections gleam on the polished obsidian mirrors — the only cold light. Background: its own place in Itsal, darker and softer than the figure, with depth: walls and towers of polished black obsidian that mirror the fire, ash drifting in the air, a night sky dark with smoke. All fifteen portraits of this set share the same framing, painting style, palette and lighting.

The enemy: the Mirror Priest, a rank-and-file debuffer of Itsal. A tall, thin sagan priest with a dark ember-crust body, a crown of flame feathers and a long ash-grey cloak. Nano Banana 2928×1152 · 4:5 · 1K · $0.0694 · 16.0 среференс, не утверждён · 2026-09-28 15:54
Промт, как он ушёл в модель
Art style: hand-painted stylized dark-fantasy game art for a mobile RPG. Painterly digital illustration with visible, confident brush strokes and simplified planar shapes, crisp rim light on edges, strong readable silhouettes, deep near-black shadows. Light tells the story: a few strong sources — cracks and salt crystals in old stone that glow from within — throw colored light upward, the light comes from below. Cold and warm light contrast. Dust motes, grains of sand and tiny sparks float in the light. Moderate detail, clean readable forms. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime, no cartoon.

Enemy card portrait, 4:5, shown small on the battle field (about 74 px wide) and large in the bestiary. Camera at chest height, waist-up: the bottom edge of the picture cuts the body at the waist — head, torso and arms in frame, no hips, no legs; the legs are never visible, whatever the pose. The figure is centered and fills most of the frame; the head sits in the upper third with a little space above it. The body is turned in a three-quarter view toward the LEFT side of the picture, where its enemies stand; its weapon, its spell or the thing it is named after is thrust toward the left and clearly shown in front of the body. It is an enemy: dangerous, moving and caught in action — not a model posing, not a statue. Its story reads from its body, its pose and the place around it. World: these are the dead of Ta-Nehem, an ancient kingdom by a river of reeds and sand. They dried their dead with salt and wrapped them in linen so that the form would not leave them, and a dead king went on ruling; then the dead kings rose with their army and marched on the living to lead them into their eternal kingdom. Their look is inspired by ancient Egypt — linen wrappings, gold masks, broad collars of gold and blue-green faience beads, striped royal headcloths, jackal-headed guards, golden scarabs, reeds and sand — but they are clearly the risen DEAD: bodies wrapped in stiff linen crusted with white salt, dark dry hands like old polished wood where the linen has slipped, and calm eyes that glow pale turquoise; dignified, eerie and ancient, never rotting, never skeletal, never gory; they must not look like real-world people or like a horror-film mummy. Walls, columns and objects are plain or carry only broad simple ornament — lotus petals, reeds, stripes, zigzags, feathers — never hieroglyphs, never rows of small signs or little pictures. Colors: muted and dry, like all our enemies — salt white, pale linen, sand ochre, dull old gold, faded turquoise and lapis faience, dark river green, near-black; everything else sinks into near-black shadow. Light, the same for the whole set: night; the light comes from below — cold pale turquoise light glowing from within salt crystals and cracks in old stone rises onto the figure; crisp cold turquoise rim light on its edges; a small warm amber glow of oil lamps, caught by the gold, is the only warm light. Background: its own place in Ta-Nehem, darker and softer than the figure, with depth. All fifteen portraits of this set share the same framing, painting style, palette and lighting.

The enemy: the Lord of Beetles, an elite debuffer of Ta-Nehem. A dead nobleman in a long pleated linen robe with very wide sleeves, a large gold scarab pectoral on his chest, a striped headcloth; his face is wrapped in linen with two pale turquoise lights for eyes. Action: he points to the left with one long finger, and out of his wide sleeves pours a stream of golden scarabs that flies through the air to the left, exactly where he points; a gust of wind and sand (Air) swirls around them. Background: a tomb gallery at night, rows of sealed jars, pale turquoise light.

No text, no letters, no numbers, no glyphs, no hieroglyphs, no real-world scripts, no carvings that look like writing or numerals, no occult symbols, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no UI elements, no border or frame around the picture. No gore, no blood, no skulls, no skeletons of people, no rotting flesh, no decay, no sacrifice, no horror grotesque.

Промт, как он ушёл в модель
Dark fantasy game art with a menacing, gloomy, mystical atmosphere. Digital painting with soft transitions, elaborate shadows and an artistic emphasis on details. Lighting effects bring it to life: magical glow, aura and embers, light that comes from inside the subject and from below. Rich worn materials: dark forged iron, old gold, weathered stone, carst crystals glowing from within. Precious, dramatic, high contrast.

Format: game UI icon of a Memory of the Wanderer, square, no border around the picture. One shard of a broken magic mirror, upright, centered, floating in the dark, about 80% of the canvas high. The shard floats on pitch black: everything around it is solid pure black to the very edges of the canvas, never white or grey. All eight icons of this set are one series with one and the same shard: the same silhouette, size and angle; only the light inside tells them apart. The silhouette: a broad jagged piece of mirror glass, about two thirds as wide as it is tall — one long sharp point at the top, a long almost straight left edge, a right edge broken into two straight segments with a small notch between them, and a jagged bottom edge that rises from the lower left corner to the lower right; straight fracture lines and sharp corners, never rounded, never drop- or almond-shaped. It is mirror glass, not a gemstone: a flat pane of thick polished glass seen straight on, its face smooth and glossy with no cut facets like a jewel; the broken edges are thick bevelled glass that catches crisp bright light, and behind the glass a thin layer of old tarnished silver — the backing of the mirror — shows along the whole broken contour as a bright silver rim. Fine hairline cracks run in from the broken edges. The face of the glass is dark and deep, like a mirror hanging in a dark room: never pale, never silvery or white — the bright silver shows only as the thin rim along the broken contour. Deep inside the glass, as if far behind its surface, lives a reflection that is a memory: blurred light and soft haze of its own color, like something remembered through mist. The eight icons form a ladder of inner light: the higher the rarity, the more of the glass this light fills and the brighter it burns — at the top of the ladder it fills the whole shard. No faces, no figures, no eyes, no text, no runes or symbols in it. The glass is never pitch black inside: even its darkest depths keep a visible tone. All the light stays inside the glass: no glow, aura or halo outside the shard, no embers — right outside its silver rim the background is pure black. A bare shard: no frame, no setting, no metal caps, no stand, no base; no other shards, splinters, sparks or particles floating around it. All the detail lives inside the silhouette. It must stay readable at a tiny size, 24 px: one bold solid shape with a clear bright outline.

Memory: Ancient, the fifth of seven. Strong deep red light (#E85A4E) fills most of the glass: far behind the surface a whirl of bright crimson flame swirls around the center and lights the whole shard red from within; the hairline cracks glow red.

The background is solid pure black (#000000), flat, edge to edge: no gradient, no texture, no floor, no cast shadow, no vignette, no checkerboard. Any glow stays close to the subject and fades into the black within a short distance. The whole icon with its glow fits inside the central 80% of the canvas in both width and height: an empty black margin of at least a tenth of the canvas stays on every side — top, bottom, left and right.

No text, no letters, no numbers, no real-world alphabets, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no UI elements.

Format: game UI icon of a Memory of the Wanderer, square, no border around the picture. One shard of a broken magic mirror, upright, centered, floating in the dark, about 80% of the canvas high. The shard floats on pitch black: everything around it is solid pure black to the very edges of the canvas, never white or grey. All eight icons of this set are one series with one and the same shard: the same silhouette, size and angle; only the light inside tells them apart. The silhouette: a broad jagged piece of mirror glass, about two thirds as wide as it is tall — one long sharp point at the top, a long almost straight left edge, a right edge broken into two straight segments with a small notch between them, and a jagged bottom edge that rises from the lower left corner to the lower right; straight fracture lines and sharp corners, never rounded, never drop- or almond-shaped. It is mirror glass, not a gemstone: a flat pane of thick polished glass seen straight on, its face smooth and glossy with no cut facets like a jewel; the broken edges are thick bevelled glass that catches crisp bright light, and behind the glass a thin layer of old tarnished silver — the backing of the mirror — shows along the whole broken contour as a bright silver rim. Fine hairline cracks run in from the broken edges. The face of the glass is dark and deep, like a mirror hanging in a dark room: never pale, never silvery or white — the bright silver shows only as the thin rim along the broken contour. Deep inside the glass, as if far behind its surface, lives a reflection that is a memory: blurred light and soft haze of its own color, like something remembered through mist. The eight icons form a ladder of inner light: the higher the rarity, the more of the glass this light fills and the brighter it burns — at the top of the ladder it fills the whole shard. No faces, no figures, no eyes, no text, no runes or symbols in it. The glass is never pitch black inside: even its darkest depths keep a visible tone. All the light stays inside the glass: no glow, aura or halo outside the shard, no embers — right outside its silver rim the background is pure black. A bare shard: no frame, no setting, no metal caps, no stand, no base; no other shards, splinters, sparks or particles floating around it. All the detail lives inside the silhouette. It must stay readable at a tiny size, 24 px: one bold solid shape with a clear bright outline.

Memory: Primordial, the sixth of seven. Orange (#EB9D40): fire burns in the depth of the reflection and fills almost the whole glass; strong warm light spills out through the hairline cracks and along the broken edges, yet no sparks or embers fly outside the glass.

The background is solid pure black (#000000), flat, edge to edge: no gradient, no texture, no floor, no cast shadow, no vignette, no checkerboard. Any glow stays close to the subject and fades into the black within a short distance. The whole icon with its glow fits inside the central 80% of the canvas in both width and height: an empty black margin of at least a tenth of the canvas stays on every side — top, bottom, left and right.

No text, no letters, no numbers, no real-world alphabets, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no UI elements.

Art style: hand-painted stylized dark-fantasy game art for a mobile RPG. Painterly digital illustration with visible, confident brush strokes and simplified planar shapes, crisp rim light on edges, strong readable silhouettes, deep near-black shadows. Epic, dramatic character art: a powerful pose, a low camera, strong theatrical light from below. Light tells the story: a few strong sources — the sand of hourglasses, cracks in the stone floor and fine grooves in old stone that glow from within — throw warm amber light upward, the light comes from below. Warm and cold light contrast. Dust motes and fine stone grit float in the light. Moderate detail, clean readable forms; the face, the hands and the weapon get the most detail. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime, no cartoon.

Draw exactly one image in a single pass: no alternative versions, no second attempts, no text in the reply. Enemy card portrait, 4:5. The card is shown small on the battle field (about 74 px wide) and large in the bestiary, so the enemy must read as one bold, simple, well-lit silhouette with a clear pose against a darker background. Framing: a close, heroic half-length portrait. The camera is a little below the figure's chest and looks slightly up, so the enemy towers over the viewer and fills most of the frame. A figure shaped like a dwarf is cut by the bottom edge of the picture at the belt: head, shoulders, chest, arms and hands in the frame, no hips, no legs, no feet. Beasts and machines are framed as their own description says. The head sits in the upper third with a little space above it. The body is turned in three-quarter view toward the LEFT side of the picture, where its enemies stand; its weapon, its spell or the thing it is named after is thrust toward the left, in front of the body, and reads clearly. Pathos: it is a worthy and dangerous enemy — powerful, proud, alive and caught at the peak of an action, a foe that is frightening and honourable to defeat. Its character shows in its face, its gaze and its posture; its story shows in the details of its body and its tools. No one in this set wears a hood. World: the Library of Ularion, the workshop of the god of knowledge deep under the city of Endalor — a real ancient library cut in dark stone. Its halls go down and down; on long stone shelves lie stone tablets and stone cylinders covered with long, straight, parallel engraved grooves, like ruled lines with nothing written between them — the writing that only the god can read shows only as this worn texture of straight lines, never as letters, squiggles or signs. On the worktables parts of dwarves and parts of mechanisms lie together: the god made the people and the machine with the same hands. At every work place stands an hourglass of bronze and glass with glowing amber sand. Stone beetles live in the shelves; stone sagans are rock that has noticed itself. The Library's servants are stone dwarves made by the god. The Library calls them puppets, but they are masterworks, made carefully and with pride: carved from dark grey stone with the precision of great sculpture, polished smooth where they move and left with fine chisel marks elsewhere; the proportions of dwarf warriors — very broad shoulders, a deep chest, a thick neck, massive forearms, big capable hands; strong individual faces with heavy brows and broad noses, carved beards bound with bronze rings; bronze ball joints — precise, well-oiled work with thin engraved bands of straight lines — at the neck, shoulders, elbows and wrists, unless the description says otherwise. Their eyes are inlaid stones that glow from within, amber unless the description says otherwise: alive, attentive, fixed on the enemy with purpose. Their hands know the work and the fight; only the writing they cannot understand. They move with weight and certainty, like veteran warriors and master craftsmen. Colors: muted, like all our enemies — dark grey basalt, warm dull bronze and old brass, soot black, dusty ochre; everything else sinks into near-black shadow. Light, the same for the whole set: the light comes from below — warm amber light from the sand of the hourglasses, from cracks in the stone floor and from the grooves of the tablets rises onto the figure and lights its face and hands from underneath; crisp cool grey-blue rim light on its edges is the only cold light. Background: its own place in the Library, darker and softer than the figure, with depth. All fourteen portraits of this set share the same framing, painting style, palette and lighting.

The enemy: the Loose One, a rank-and-file skirmisher of the Library (Earth). Who he is: a lean, wiry stone dwarf whose bronze joints have worked loose over the centuries — and he has found a use for it: one of his arms unfolds like a carpenter's folding ruler and reaches farther than any blade. Right now he is reaching past the heroes' front line for the one who is already wounded. Character: sly, twitchy and predatory — a scavenger who always picks the weakest. His head hangs tilted on a loose neck joint at a hungry angle, one amber eye narrowed and the other wide open, the corner of his carved mouth pulled up in a crooked, knowing grin. Pose, the moment of the reach: he leans his upper body far forward toward the left, low, the shoulder of his reaching arm pushed ahead. That arm shoots out toward the left and unfolds in a zigzag of six straight stone segments joined by small bronze hinges, stretching almost to the left edge of the picture; at its end a stone hand with long sharpened stone fingers is spread like a claw, about to seize. His other arm hangs loose at his side, the hand dangling from a slack wrist joint. He has exactly two arms, both attached at the shoulders. Details that tell his story: (1) his loose joints rattle, and little puffs of stone dust shake out of them as he moves; (2) one hinge pin is missing and has been replaced with a bent bronze nail; (3) each segment of the folding arm has small evenly spaced notches along its edge, like a measuring rule, without any numbers; (4) his fingertips are filed to points; (5) his short beard is ragged and chipped at the ends. Place: a high gallery of the Library at the edge of a dark drop, stone tablets knocked off a shelf by his arm and falling; amber light glowing from the cracks of the floor below.

Who it is: a stone sagan — a swarm of grey grit and sharp chips of broken tablets that has noticed itself and learned that it can be someone. Its face is formed out of hundreds of small stones: a sharp brow, deep hollows for eyes with amber light burning far inside, and an open mouth from which ribbons of fine grit pour out and are sucked back in — it whispers without pause. Pose, the peak of the spell: it rises to its full height and flings both arms up and wide toward the left; above the left side of the picture a storm of stones gathers in the air and begins to fall in a heavy rockfall onto its enemies (Earth). Its head is thrown slightly back, its chest open, stones streaming from its shoulders into the storm. Details that tell its story: (1) among the grit spin fragments of broken stone tablets with fine grooves on them — it is made of the Library's broken writings, and it whispers them; (2) warm amber light pulses in the gaps between its stones like a heartbeat; (3) its edges keep crumbling and gathering again, fine dust trailing off in spirals; (4) a few larger chips circle its head like a crown. Place: a hall where a whole stone shelf has collapsed, a heap of broken tablets below it; dust hangs in the amber light rising from the cracks of the floor.

Place: a narrow repair niche of the Library with pegs of spare bronze joints on the wall and an hourglass whose amber sand has almost run out; oil stains on the stone floor, amber light from the cracks below.

The enemy: the Erased, a rare and deadly assassin of the Library (Air). Who she is: a stone dwarf woman from whom every mark was scraped off long ago, and her name and her work were erased with them. Now it is as if she does not exist. She walks without a sound between the shelves and comes out right at the one who heals. Right now she has chosen the heroes' healer. Character: cold, silent, patient and merciless — absence used as a weapon. A thin cold draught (Air) follows her and pulls a trail of dust out of the gap behind her. Details that tell her story: (1) her whole pale grey stone body is covered with long parallel scrape marks — even her cheek and brow — everything was scraped smooth, not one sign is left; (2) her bronze joints are tightly wrapped in dark cloth so they make no sound; (3) the erasing knife is worn thin and curved like a crescent from centuries of scraping; (4) her hair is carved close to her head in smooth, simple bands, scraped smooth like the rest; (5) she is half in shadow — the light finds only her face, the knife and the edge of her shoulder. Place: the dark gap between two tall stone shelves; on the nearest shelf lies a stone tablet scraped completely blank; faint amber light rises from the floor below, and a cold grey-blue light runs along her edges.

The enemy: the Fitter, an elite brawler of the Library (Earth). Who he is: the master fitter of the Library's worktables, a heavy, powerful stone dwarf with a bronze hammer and a box of joints. Character: confident, brutal and practical, with a craftsman's pride — he is not angry, he is working. His brows are lowered in concentration, his amber eyes measure the target coldly, his mouth is set in a grim, satisfied line. Details that tell his story: (1) the hammer has a long handle wound with worn leather, its bronze face dented by a thousand blows; (2) a wide leather strap across his chest holds a battered wooden box of spare bronze joints at his hip; (3) his own body is fitted from mismatched parts — one forearm is of a lighter stone than the rest, joined at the elbow with a newer bronze ring: he fitted himself; (4) bronze calipers hang from his belt; (5) his long braided beard is tucked into his belt so it does not catch in the work. Place: a long worktable of the Library behind him with stone arms, hands and gears laid out in neat rows and a half-assembled stone dwarf lying on it; an hourglass with glowing amber sand; amber light glowing in the cracks of the floor below.

Place: an archive hall of the Library where knotted cords hang from the ceiling like heavy curtains; amber light from the cracks of the floor below.

Subject: Astrid Half-Grosh, a woman of the northern lands, a warrior of great strength of the Fire school. Who she is: of the northern women, only three in a generation go to the arena sands and on campaigns, and the north knew her by her second blade — a fire stone was set into it when she was twenty. On the campaign against the southern elven forest the jarl gave her the purse of the campaign: the second halves of split coins for the hired strangers, who had taken the first halves in advance. On the third day the forest paths began to go in circles. She was afraid, like everyone — and she went on. Character: steadfast, honest and fierce; fear burned away by fire, duty kept to the last. Her face: early thirties, weathered and freckled, a strong jaw, a thin white scar across one cheekbone, fierce grey eyes with the scarlet glow of the stone reflected in them, lips drawn back over gritted teeth in a battle cry; ash-blond hair in thick northern braids, a few loose strands whipped by the heat. Pose, the moment of the charge: she charges toward the right, her weight thrown onto her leading shoulder, her torso twisting into the swing. Her near hand holds a broad northern sword low and back, ready to sweep up; her far hand raises the second blade high above her shoulder — a shorter, heavy blade with a scarlet fire stone set at the base of the blade, glowing like a coal, flames licking along its edge (Fire). Her head is lowered, chin tucked, eyes fixed on the enemy beyond the right edge. Details that tell her story: (1) at her belt hangs a heavy leather purse tied tight with a thong, a few dull half-coins with jagged broken edges glinting at its mouth — she never lets go of it; (2) a mail shirt under a sleeveless fur-trimmed leather jerkin, a wide belt; (3) old burn scars on the wrist and forearm of the hand that holds the fire blade; (4) a thin iron torc at her neck; (5) forest mist curling around her and dead leaves torn up by her charge. Place: a dark primeval elven forest where the paths go in circles: colossal twisted trees and huge roots, mist, a path that loops back on itself behind her. Scarlet-red light of the Fire school rises from glowing embers among the roots below and from her blade; cold mist beyond.

Subject: Elias, a homeless archer of the roads, a human man, a swift archer of the Air school. Who he is: he guarded caravans for food and never asked where they went. On a southern road he carried a fallen elven wanderer into the shade, and she gave him a scroll that would admit him to the great Tree of the elves. He did not go to the Tree — he went after her. With her small band he walked the old roads, and for the first time he had a home, only it was always on the move. He learned to shoot so quietly that he never woke the sleepers in camp. Character: quiet, restrained and loyal to the end — a man of few words who has found something to protect. His face: in his thirties, lean and weathered, a short dark beard, dark hair tied back, a thin scar through one eyebrow, calm dark eyes utterly focused; his lips pressed together, holding his breath. Pose, the moment before the shot: he stands between the sleeping camp and the dark, his body turned toward the right, and draws a long plain bow to full draw toward the right; the fletching touches the corner of his mouth, the drawing elbow is high behind him, the bow arm straight and steady; his head is tilted slightly to the arrow, eyes on the enemy beyond the right edge. A thin thread of white-green wind (Air) winds silently around the arrowhead. Details that tell his story: (1) a rolled scroll tied with a stem of dry grass is tucked under the strap across his chest, its seal unbroken — he never unrolled it; (2) small tufts of wool are bound onto his bowstring so it makes no sound; (3) a caravan guard's worn leather bracer on his bow arm and a road-worn, much-patched grey cloak; (4) mismatched arrows in his quiver, fletched with feathers of different birds gathered on the road; (5) a bedroll strapped across his back. Place: an ancient paved road at night beside a ruined roadside station of pale stone; behind him, small and warm, a campfire, and around it the dark shapes of his sleeping companions under blankets. Pale white-green light of the Air school rises from cracks between the old paving stones below; road dust drifts in the light.

Subject: Vetverog, a sentient beast of the southern elven forest, a warrior of great strength of the Air school. Who he is: in the elven forest there are beasts that the Watchers raise with a single word. No one ever raised him: he came out to the fire of the two-legged wanderers by himself and lay down beside it — he decided, not the herd. He walked with them to the end, and when the last of them, the archer, was laid by the road, he lay down beside him and went no further. Character: proud, free and loyal by his own choice — a wild lord of the forest with a thinking mind. His eyes are deep amber-gold and intelligent, fierce now, the eyes of someone who remembers and defends. Appearance: a colossal forest stag-beast, far bigger than an elk, with a heavy mane of grey-brown fur on his neck and chest and a crown of enormous antlers, wider than a man is tall, that branch like the limbs of an old tree — pale as bone, with moss and a few small living leaves growing on them. Framing and pose, the moment of the challenge: he is a beast, and the half-body frame is close: his head, his antlers, his neck, his chest and his front legs fill the frame, and the rest of his body is out of the frame. The camera is low and looks up at him. He rears up toward the right on his hind legs, his forelegs lifted high and striking the air, his head turned toward the right and his mouth open in a roaring bellow; his breath bursts out toward the right as a gust of white-green wind (Air) that whirls leaves around his great antlers; the muscles of his neck and chest stand out under the mane. Details that tell his story: (1) a thin braided cord of dry grass is tied around one tine of his antlers — a token from the healer who touched each companion every evening as if counting them; (2) the fur of his chest is darkened with the smoke of many campfires; (3) an old notch in one ear and a pale scar across his muzzle; (4) one antler tine is broken off short and has healed smooth; (5) embers from a campfire drift around him. Place: the edge of an ancient elven forest by a dusty road at dusk, a small campfire glowing behind him. Pale white-green light of the Air school rises from the roots and the earth below; leaves and sparks drift in the air.

Subject: Oelis the Unlayering, a woman of a forgotten people who lived long before all the cities that stand today, a controller and battle mage of the Time school. Who she is: her people were as many as the stars over the river, and every craft had its own key — not a word, but the way you hold your hand. Her key was to take the years off things, layer by layer, the way bark is peeled, until the new showed through under the old: a cracked wall came out of her hands whole, a black bowl came out bright as on the day it was fired. Their city stood by the water and was built of white clay. Once she was asked to take the years off a person, and she tried — under the years a person has nothing new, only the same, shorter; she pulled her hands back and never tried again. The last thing she renewed was the bowl in which her people's fire burned. Character: grave, sorrowful and unbending — the last of her people, who knows exactly what her power costs and uses it without hesitation. A timeless, majestic presence: a legend. Her face: ageless and striking, unlike any people living now — a long neck, a long narrow face with high cheekbones, large almond-shaped eyes with luminous green irises; her skin has the warm grey-brown tone of river clay; long straight black hair falls to her waist, bound at intervals with small rings of white fired clay; fine lines of white clay are painted along her brow and cheekbones. Pose, the moment of the spell: the camera is low; she stands tall, turned toward the right, her head high, her gaze level, hard and sorrowful. Her near arm is thrust out toward the right, the hand open and the fingers hooked as if gripping the edge of something invisible — and she tears it back: from the enemy beyond the right edge long curling layers of green light peel away toward her like strips of bark, one after another, and crumble into motes in the air (Time); the wind of it lifts her hair and her sleeves. Her far hand holds a shallow clay bowl close to her chest, and a small flame burns in it. Details that tell her story: (1) the bowl is of white clay, bright and new as on the day it was fired, while its foot is still black and cracked — it is being renewed layer by layer; (2) her hands are dusted with white clay up to the wrists; (3) a robe of undyed pale linen with a wide collar of white clay beads; (4) a small whistle of bone hangs on a cord at her throat; (5) the hem of her sleeves frays into fine pale flakes that curl and drift away like peeled layers. Place: the ruins of an ancient city of white clay beside a wide dark river under a sky full of stars. Green light of the Time school rises from the water and from cracks in the old clay below; motes of light drift in the air.

Rich worn materials: dark forged iron, old gold, weathered stone, carst crystals glowing from within. Precious, dramatic, high contrast.

Format: game UI icon of an equipment slot, square, no border around the picture. One item of equipment, centered, about 80% of the canvas, seen straight on or in a clear three-quarter view. The item is empty and stands alone: nobody wears or holds it. The item floats on pitch black: everything around it is solid pure black to the very edges of the canvas, never white or grey, no frame. It must stay readable at a tiny size, 24 px: one simple, strong, instantly recognizable silhouette built from a few large shapes with clear contrast between them. All the painterly detail lives inside the silhouette — worn metal, leather, rivets, scratches, light — never as small separate pieces around it: no sparks, embers, shards or particles floating around the item. A crisp pale rim light runs along the whole outline and cleanly separates it from the black. The item is rarity-neutral: its materials are dark forged iron, blackened steel, worn dark leather and dark stone, with only thin accents of dull old gold; no bright colors, no colored gems, no colored glow — the interface adds the color of rarity around the icon. Dark materials are never pitch black: even the darkest iron and leather keep a visible dark tone with worn highlights, clearly lighter than the background. The light on the item is neutral: a pale warm light from below, subdued. No runes, glyphs or symbols drawn on it. The nine icons are one set: the same painting style, the same neutral light and the same size in the frame; only the silhouette tells them apart.

A helmet: an open-faced nasal helm in a three-quarter view, turned slightly to the right: a rounded, slightly pointed dome of dark forged iron made of riveted plates, one broad nose guard running straight down the front, a thin band of dull old gold around the brow, and a short curtain of dark chainmail hanging at the back and the sides of the neck. Through the open face the worn dark leather lining inside the helm is dimly visible — never a black hole. Not a closed great helm: no visor, no eye slit, no crest. Sturdy and simple.

The background is solid pure black (#000000), flat, edge to edge: no gradient, no texture, no floor, no cast shadow, no vignette, no checkerboard. Any glow stays close to the subject and fades into the black within a short distance. The whole icon with its glow fits inside the central 80% of the canvas in both width and height: an empty black margin of at least a tenth of the canvas stays on every side — top, bottom, left and right.

No text, no letters, no numbers, no real-world alphabets, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no UI elements.

It stands upright and straight: its long axis is vertical — not tilted, not leaning, never a slanted rhombus or parallelogram. Everything around it is solid pure black to the very edges of the canvas, never white or grey. The silhouette: a broad jagged piece of mirror glass, about four fifths as wide as it is tall and widest in its middle, with a large calm middle where a face could be reflected — one sharp point at the top, a little right of the center; a long, almost straight left edge; a right edge broken into two straight segments with a small notch between them; a jagged bottom edge that rises from the lower left corner to the lower right. Straight fracture lines and sharp corners, never rounded, never drop- or almond-shaped. It is the ghost of a mirror: the same broken mirror glass as a shard of Memory, but not quite there — spectral and translucent, made of cold pale light and mist. Only its contour is solid: a thin bevelled edge of pale tarnished silver, the backing of the mirror, runs along the whole broken contour and catches a crisp cold light. Soft pale mist clings to this rim and frays into faint smoky wisps along the broken edges, drifting a little inward over the glass; within a short distance the mist fades into black. A few faint hairline cracks run in from the edges. The whole middle of the shard is empty: a pure black void, as black as the background, where nothing is reflected yet — no face, no figure, no eyes, no reflection, no light and no haze in the middle. The ghost light is a cold pale silver with a faint turquoise tint (#BFEFEA): never green, never warm, never golden. No glow, aura or halo spreading outside the shard; no other shards, splinters, sparks or particles around it. A bare shard: no frame, no setting, no metal caps, no stand, no base. It must stay readable at a small size, 32 px: one bold jagged outline with a clear pale edge.

A hero shard, empty: a hero's soul is being gathered into this mirror piece by piece, but for now the mirror still holds nothing. The pale silver rim is thin and even along the whole contour; the mist is thickest at the corners and thinnest along the straight edges; the black void inside is large and clean, taking up most of the shard.

The background is solid pure black (#000000), flat, edge to edge: no gradient, no texture, no floor, no cast shadow, no vignette, no checkerboard. All four talismans of this set are one series: the same materials, the same painting style, the same size in the frame; only the shape of the charm and the color of its inner light tell them apart. Every talisman of the series is a flat carved charm of dark materials — dark forged iron, dark carved bone, dark leather or dark stone — with fittings of worn old gold; a short loop of knotted dark cord rises from its top, for wearing it on the body; and in its heart sits one smooth oval cabochon of milky moonstone lit from inside by the captured soul-trait: a small ghostly swirl of colored light, like a wisp of smoke, turning inside the stone. The same inner light catches the nearest edges of the charm from within. The light stays inside the charm: no glow, aura or halo outside it, no embers, sparks or particles floating around. It must stay readable at a tiny size, 24 px: one simple, strong, instantly recognizable silhouette built from a few large shapes; all the painterly detail lives inside the silhouette. A crisp bright rim light runs along the whole outline and cleanly separates it from the black. Dark materials are never pitch black: they keep a visible dark tone with worn highlights, clearly lighter than the background. No runes, letters, glyphs, sigils or occult signs anywhere on it.

Family: Seal talismans — traits of refusal and warding, of how a soul would not let a curse take hold. The charm: a square seal-plaque of dark stone standing on one corner like a diamond, with a thick bevelled rim of old gold; in its center a round seal of old gold with a wavy edge, like metal pressed while molten; the moonstone is set as the face of the seal. The soul-light is a cold turquoise (#48E5D4) — a ward — glowing inside the moonstone and in a few fine cracks of the dark stone around it.

The background is solid pure black (#000000), flat, edge to edge: no gradient, no texture, no floor, no cast shadow, no vignette, no checkerboard. Any glow stays close to the subject and fades into the black within a short distance. The whole icon with its glow fits inside the central 80% of the canvas in both width and height: an empty black margin of at least a tenth of the canvas stays on every side — top, bottom, left and right.

No text, no letters, no numbers, no real-world alphabets, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no UI elements.

Subject: Endalor, the flying city of mages, the heart of the world, seen from a little below and to the side at dusk. Who it is: an enormous disc of a city that hangs high above a sea of clouds over the great chasm in the middle of the world; it has no land of its own. Its underside is a massive machine belly of dark iron and stone: great supports with glowing blue accumulator cells, huge hanging chains, gears, rows of lights shining down into the clouds. The city burns green crystal every second, and a steady green glow pours from its underside down onto the clouds, visible from far away. On top: a fortress wall with long banners runs around the rim; above the wall rise the quarters of five schools of magic, each in its own color and style, and above each quarter floats a large symbol of its element, made of glowing crystal and light like an old enchanted sculpture, not a flat icon: a drop of water glowing blue; an hourglass of green crystal with green sand pouring through its waist — an hourglass, not a clock: no clock face, no dial, no hands, no arrows; a boulder glowing amber; a whirlwind glowing white-green; a flame glowing scarlet. Three landmarks, each appearing exactly once: one single great building shaped like two gigantic stone hands holding up an open book with blank stone pages — there is only one such building in the whole city; one black obelisk without windows or doors, the tallest thing in the city, like a hole cut out of the picture, and its sharp tip stands fully inside the picture with open sky above it; one small round ring of stone for duels between mages. At one edge, a dark heavy quarter of the dwarves with chimneys and smoke. Far below, through a break in the clouds, the dark mouth of a chasm in the earth — only darkness inside, nothing at all can be seen in its depth. Light: the main light comes from below — the green glow from the city's underside lights the clouds and the city's rim from beneath; warm golden windows; a cold blue dusk sky above. Composition: the whole city disc is seen from a distance and fits inside the picture with sky around it, filling the middle band, slightly left of center; the black obelisk rises above the skyline and its tip is well below the top edge; clouds and the dark chasm below; the lower part of the picture is darker. Mood: awe, old magic, hidden machinery.

Subject: Norden-Vild, the fortress city of the harsh north, seen from the sea on a winter night. An enormous fortress of dark stone on a rocky sea shore, with concentric walls and quarters laid out in rings. In the very center lies a great open arena of sand, a colosseum, and from it the rings spread outward: nearest to the sand the heavy stone houses of the jarls, farther out the long houses with turf roofs, barracks, the market and the quarter for strangers. Above the city rises a cliff, and cut into it is the Temple of Fire: a portal of massive columns, a long stair climbing up to it and an open flame burning in the doorway, seen from the sea and from the mountains. Subject: Vial, the first of the five gods, god of air, the sculptor of the world. Who he is: when the world was one formless substance, he divided it into lands — mountains, waters, deserts, forests and steppes — and with the same movement shaped the living bodies: people, elves, dwarves, beasts and plants. He made the vessels in which life became possible. He alone of the five came to love what he made. Right now he has just finished shaping a small living thing and lets it go into the world. Character: warm, attentive and patient, with a master craftsman's tenderness; a quiet, kind smile at the corners of his mouth, gentle eyes following the creature he has just released; an unhurried, generous bearing. His face: an ageless man with fine features, wind-blown light hair and a short beard. Pose, the moment of release: he stands tall with his weight on his back foot, his torso turned slightly to the right; his near hand is raised open at shoulder height, and from his palm a small pale bird, still the color of fresh clay, has just come alive and takes off in a swirl of white-green wind; his far hand holds a tall, slender bow of pale wood upright against his shoulder. His head is inclined toward the bird. He has exactly two arms: the near arm raised with the open palm, the far arm holding the bow. Details that tell his story: (1) his sleeves are rolled up, and his forearms and fingers are smudged with pale clay — he still works with his hands; (2) a long wanderer's robe of pale grey-green, the hood thrown back onto his shoulders, its hem torn and lifted by the wind; (3) the bowstring glows faintly white-green, and a few arrows sit in a simple quiver at his hip; (4) behind him thin streams of sand pour down from above like the columns of an hourglass nobody turns; (5) white-green crystals glow from within in the rocks at his feet. Place: a high cliff above a newly shaped land — below spread mountains, rivers, forests and steppes, some of the farthest still soft and unfinished like wet clay; white-green light rises from the crystals below; morning mist and wind.

Subject: the Altar of Soul Rebirth — a vast round sanctum hewn in black stone deep underground, where lost souls are called back. In the center, set upright on a low stepped altar of black marble veined with turquoise, stands a great round mirror about half the picture high, in a heavy ring frame of tarnished silver and old gold carved with a wreath of flowing wisps; its surface is deep turquoise soul-glass with a slow whirl of pale mist inside, glowing from within. Tall pillars of black stone ring the sanctum and recede into darkness; between them hang heavy curtains of deep teal velvet with old gold fringe. On both sides small silver braziers burn with cold turquoise flames, and a few hanging lamps of old gold give warm light high above. From long cracks in the altar steps and the floor turquoise light rises upward and lights the pillars and the mirror frame from below. Pale motes of soul-light drift upward toward the mirror like slow snow in reverse. Regal, sacred, mysterious — a place where something precious returns.

The hero belongs to the people of the river reeds — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today, in endless reed marshes and on the earthen dams of a great slow river, downstream from the stepped towers of An-Keshar. They look unlike any people living now: tall, long-limbed and light like herons, with long narrow faces, high cheekbones and large, calm eyes of pale grey-green, the colour of river water; their skin is a deep olive-brown with a faint silvery sheen, like wet river silt; their dark hair is bleached pale at the ends by sun and water and bound in a long knot with reed cord; they paint thin wavy lines of pale grey river clay across their shoulders, forearms and cheekbones, like ripples on water. They wear short wraps and kilts of woven reed fibre and undyed linen, capes of plaited reed and belts of twisted reed; ornaments of freshwater shell, fish bone and small river pearls; their tools are simple — reed, bone, black river pitch, fired clay and a little copper; their boats and their arched houses are bundles of tall reeds. They measure the year by the water, from the great flood to the low water. Their enemies were the star-gazers of An-Keshar — spearmen in bronze helmets and bronze scale, priests in robes of deep lapis blue who sang the names of the nights, light war chariots, banners with winged lions and small gold star rosettes, stepped towers of fired brick faced with blue glazed brick far away on the horizon; such things appear only as trophies or as the threat beyond the right edge.

Subject: Kiddu Star-Fighter, a man of the river reeds, a battle mage of the Time school. Who he is: as a boy he was traded to a tower of An-Keshar for a boat of reeds, to carry water up to the priests on the highest step; there he learned to read the sky from scraps of their songs, and his count of the nights ran further than theirs. He read the night of the invasion before the priests did, and met them where their own sky pointed: he sang their song with his own count and led the bronze ranks into the lowland below the dam. Right now he turns their own stars against them. Character: brilliant, bitter and unforgiving — a cold certainty: he knows the sky better than those who taught it; his head lifted, his eyes reflecting the stars, his mouth open in a low chant. Pose, the moment of the spell: the camera is low; he stands on the dam at night, turned toward the right, his long body stretched tall. Green motes of light fall around him like slow sand. Details that tell his story: (1) an old clay water jar hangs on a cord across his back — the jar he carried up the tower as a boy; (2) the cord of knots and pebbles is very long and wound twice around his wrist; (3) his hair is grey at the temples and bound with reed cord; (4) thin wavy clay lines on his cheekbones; (5) a scrap of faded blue cloth is wound around the neck of the jar. Place: the dam above a flooded lowland at night under a vast sky crowded with stars; far away on the horizon, a dark stepped tower of brick with no fire at its top. The hero belongs to the valley weavers — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today, in a green mountain valley below the terraced mountains of Hatun-Rumi. Everything they own is woven: clothes, belts, slings, shields and the rope bridges over the gorges. They look unlike any people living now: slight, wiry and light-boned, with long, very nimble fingers; round faces with wide cheekbones, small chins and large, clear eyes of pale gold; their skin is a warm tawny brown; their hair is naturally the colour of undyed wool — cream, grey and pale fawn even in the young — and they wear it in many thin braids tied with bits of coloured yarn. They wear tunics and mantles of hand-woven wool in bold stripes and stepped bands of rust red, ochre, indigo and cream — patterns only, never signs; woven belts, bone needles, spindles, bronze knives and braided grass ropes. Their enemies were the stone lords of Hatun-Rumi — short, very stocky mountain dwarves with long beards braided and bound with knotted cords, who carried stone shields and woollen slings, wrote nothing and kept every debt in knots on long cords, and built walls of huge many-sided stones fitted without mortar; such things appear only as trophies or as the threat beyond the right edge.

Subject: Tikku Bridge-Cutter, a man of the valley weavers, a controller of the Air school. Who he is: in the valley everyone weaves, and he wove the rope bridges himself — so he knew rope better than those who crossed it. When the masons of Hatun-Rumi came down into the valley over the rope bridges, barefoot and fast, with stones on their backs, he cut six bridges in one night, and the seventh at dawn, when the runners were already in the middle. Right now his knife is in the last rope of the seventh bridge. Character: quick, fearless and cold with anger — he hates the knot on the priests' cord that said the valley was already theirs; his teeth bared, his pale-gold eyes narrowed and fixed on the bridge beyond the right edge. Pose, the moment of the cut: the camera is low; he leans low over the anchor post of a rope bridge on the edge of a gorge, turned toward the right, his whole body driven into the stroke. He has exactly two arms: his far hand grips the thick braided grass rope where it is tied to the wooden anchor post; his near hand has just slashed a short bronze knife through it, and the cut rope springs apart in a burst of fibres. The bridge swings away toward the right over the abyss, and a gust of pale white-green wind of the Air school howls up out of the gorge, whipping the loose ropes and his braids. Details that tell his story: (1) the rope is his own weaving — thick braided grass, its fibres springing apart at the cut; (2) his fingers are calloused from the loom, a cut rope-end is tucked in his belt; (3) the handle of the bronze knife is wrapped in striped wool; (4) a hewn, square slinger's stone flies past his head from the right; (5) a coil of spare rope over his shoulder. Place: a deep gorge at dawn: the swaying rope bridge stretching away over the misty abyss, terraces of fitted grey stone and snowy peaks on the far side, a pale sky. Pale white-green light of the Air school rises from the depth of the gorge below.

When her river pebbles ran out on the first day, she began to gather the stones of the enemy — hewn and even, as if taken from a wall — and sent them back to those who threw them; people said her stones went home. At night she climbed the mortarless wall the enemy had built, where there is nothing for a finger to hold, onto a ledge above their slingers. The hero belongs to the kurgan people — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today on the endless steppe of feather grass, and raised great grassy mounds, kurgans, over their dead so that the steppe would know where they lie. They look unlike any people living now: tall, heavy-boned and broad in the shoulder, with long heads, strong jaws, heavy brows and deep-set eyes of pale amber; their skin is weathered grey-bronze, like dry steppe earth; men and women alike wear their dark hair in one heavy rope-like braid and a thin band of dull bronze around the brow. They wear long coats and trousers of felt and sheepskin, wide leather belts, toggles of bone and horn and beads of amber; their tools are bronze, horn, bone and braided horsehair. Their enemies were the Horde of the Golden Stag — intelligent beasts of the steppe, great deer, wolves, boars and griffins that spoke like people, their antlers and tusks sheathed in gold, gold plaques with stags and griffins on their chests; they crossed the land in great migrations and trampled everything in their way; such things appear only as trophies or as the threat beyond the right edge.

Subject: Targym of the Kurgan, a man of the kurgan people, a defender of the Earth school. Who he is: the great migration of the Horde swept over his camp in one morning and carried away everything but the dead. Over them he heaped a kurgan — right across the path, with earth from under the hooves — and stood on it; the second herd flowed around the mound like water around a stone: beasts do not trample graves, though they trample the living. Right now a boar-guard of the Horde charges up the mound at him. Character: grim, grieving and utterly immovable; his jaw set, his brows lowered, his amber eyes steady and full of hatred, fixed on the boar beyond the right edge. Pose, the moment of the charge: the camera is low; he stands on top of the fresh mound, turned toward the right, his shoulders driven forward. He has exactly two arms: his near arm braces a great round shield of thick layered bull-hide toward the right against the charge; his far hand grips the handle of a long wooden spade driven into the mound beside him. Amber-orange light of the Earth school bursts from cracks in the fresh earth, and clods fly up around the shield. Details that tell his story: (1) the fresh earth on his spade and hands is full of hoof-prints; (2) a long gash along his side is bound with a strip of felt; (3) his hands and forearms are black with earth to the elbows; (4) a broken boar tusk ringed with gold is stuck in the shield; (5) behind him the stampede of the Horde flows past the mound, a river of antlers and dust in soft focus. Place: the night steppe of feather grass under a pale moon, the dust of the migration hanging in the air, a lone standing stone beside the mound. Amber light rises from the cracks in the earth below; cold moonlight on his shoulders.

The hero belongs to the kurgan people — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today on the endless steppe of feather grass, and raised great grassy mounds, kurgans, over their dead so that the steppe would know where they lie. They look unlike any people living now: tall, heavy-boned and broad in the shoulder, with long heads, strong jaws, heavy brows and deep-set eyes of pale amber; their skin is weathered grey-bronze, like dry steppe earth; men and women alike wear their dark hair in one heavy rope-like braid and a thin band of dull bronze around the brow. They wear long coats and trousers of felt and sheepskin, wide leather belts, toggles of bone and horn and beads of amber; their tools are bronze, horn, bone and braided horsehair. Their enemies were the Horde of the Golden Stag — intelligent beasts of the steppe, great deer, wolves, boars and griffins that spoke like people, their antlers and tusks sheathed in gold, gold plaques with stags and griffins on their chests; they crossed the land in great migrations and trampled everything in their way; such things appear only as trophies or as the threat beyond the right edge.

Subject: Oisu, Archer of the Kurgan, a man of the kurgan people, a swift archer of the Air school. Who he is: from the top of Targym's kurgan he could see the whole herd, and the herd could not reach him — beasts do not trample the mound of the dead. He climbed it with a bow and three quivers and shot the griffins of the Horde out of the sky; his arrows were found on the steppe for ages after. Right now a griffin dives at him out of the sky from the right. Character: cold, proud and unrelenting — he has chosen to shoot the herd from above and does not care that the old ones call it unfair; his eyes narrowed along the arrow, his jaw hard. Pose, the moment of the shot: the camera is low; he stands on the top of the kurgan, turned toward the right, leaning back, the bow drawn high toward the upper right. He has exactly two arms: his near arm holds a heavy recurved bow of horn and wood raised toward the upper right; his far hand draws the string back to his ear, the arrow aimed at a griffin beyond the upper right edge. A spiral of pale white-green wind of the Air school winds around the arrow and pulls at his braid. Details that tell his story: (1) three quivers at his back and hip, one of them already empty; (2) his arrow shafts are slightly uneven — crooked shafts straightened by hand; (3) long tawny griffin feathers are tied to his quiver as trophies; (4) deep claw scratches across his leather shoulder guard; (5) below him the grass of the mound and the dust of the herd flowing past. Place: the top of a great kurgan at night under a huge moon; the migration of the Horde a river of antlers and gold in the dust below; the dark shape of spread griffin wings against the moon at the edge of the sky. Pale white-green light of the Air school rises from the grass of the mound below; cold moonlight rims his figure.
