The hero belongs to the people of the ash plains — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today, on wide plains of grey ash and black basalt, where cold is more precious than water and water is more precious than anything. They look unlike any people living now: lean and sinewy, long-limbed, with long faces, sharp cheekbones and narrow, heavy-lidded eyes of pale ice-grey; their skin is dark slate-grey with a cool bluish undertone, like cooled basalt; their hair is naturally ash-white, cropped short or worn in short thick locks tied with grey cord. They wear loose wraps and hooded mantles of undyed grey cotton and pale woven fibre and cords of grey stone beads; their tools are black basalt, grey stone, obsidian flakes, woven fibre and fired clay. Their enemies were the people of Itsal — beings of living fire held in a human-like shape, their bodies a crust of cracked charcoal and obsidian with orange-gold fire glowing through every crack, with gold sun discs and polished black obsidian mirrors, feathered serpents of flame and dogs of smouldering coal; on the Night of the Falling Suns they came down from their cities of black mirrors to warm themselves with the warmth of others; such things appear only as trophies or as the threat beyond the right edge.

Subject: Iyana Ash-Water, a woman of the ash plains, a healer of the Water school. Who she is: a burn is healed with cold, but on the ash plains cold must first be found; she found it in ash — ash stirred into water and left to settle makes the water soft and cold, like water from a deep well. The white ash that the fiery ones left behind healed best of all — the first bitterness of that night. Right now the burned are carried to her shelter, and she pours cold ash-water. Character: steady, bitter and tireless — a healer who has not stepped near a fire since that night; her face grave and tight, her eyes fixed on the burn she is cooling. Pose, the moment of healing: the camera is low; she stands under a low awning of woven fibre, turned toward the right, leaning forward. She has exactly two arms: her near arm tips a wide clay jar, and a stream of pale, milky, glowing cold ash-water pours out toward the right onto the burned beyond the right edge, cool mist rolling off it; her far hand holds a wet cloth ready. Cool blue light of the Water school shines through the stream. Details that tell her story: (1) her arms are grey with ash to the elbows; (2) rows of clay jars stand behind her, the ash settling in them; (3) soaked cloths hang drying on the poles of the awning; (4) a string of grey stone beads is wound around her wrist; (5) her back is turned to the red glow of a fallen sun on the horizon. Place: her shelter on the ash plain in a night without day: ash falling like snow, a dull red glow under a sky black with smoke. Blue light rises from the jars and the wet ground below.

The hero belongs to the people of one face — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today, in a walled city of sun-dried brick on a green river plain, not far from the gates of Meshen-Gar. A person of this people has one face and one name for life, and at the city gate everyone names themselves aloud. They look unlike any people living now: their faces are bare, calm and strongly drawn — broad brows, straight noses, full lips and very large, steady eyes of clear dark amber; their skin is a warm olive-gold with a smooth matte look, like fine clay; the men keep short trimmed beards, the women wear their dark hair in one plain braid; none of them ever wears a mask or paints the face. They wear long plain robes and wraps of undyed wool and linen with a single coloured band at the hem, wide leather belts and simple bronze; their city has walls of sun-dried brick and gates of heavy cedar beams. Their enemies were the Many-Faced of Meshen-Gar — people who changed their own bodies at will, growing wings, horns, stone skin or a second face; winged bulls with the faces of men guarded their gates, and their priests wore masks over masks; in the Tide of Forms they spread over the land like a flood of violet mist and took the face of everyone they touched; such things appear only as trophies or as the threat beyond the right edge.

Subject: Kersu Form-Holder, a man of the people of one face, a controller of the Time school. Who he is: he sat at the city gate as a scribe and remembered everyone who ever came in — even the traders from Meshen-Gar, who changed their faces the way his people change a belt. When the Tide of Forms began, the Many-Faced came against the city wearing the faces of those they had touched in the fields; he went out to them and called them by the names they had once given at the gate, and for a moment their shape held. Right now a shifting shape comes at him, and he calls out its old name. Character: steadfast, sorrowful and fearless — a quiet keeper of names who hates the familiar faces most, because he remembers how they smiled; his brows drawn, his mouth open in a loud call, his amber eyes wide and fierce. Pose, the moment of the spell: the camera is low; he stands before the gate, turned toward the right, leaning forward into a wind that whips his robe back. He has exactly two arms: his near arm is thrust out toward the right, the finger pointing, and a ring of green light of the Time school shoots from his hand and closes around a shape of shifting violet mist beyond the right edge, holding it still for a moment; his far hand is clenched at his chest around a reed stylus. Details that tell his story: (1) his fingers are stained with dried clay from years at the gate; (2) a second reed stylus is tucked behind his ear; (3) a closed wooden writing board hangs at his hip on a cord; (4) a plain robe with a single blue band at the hem; (5) a grey feather from a changed one's wing is caught on his sleeve. Place: the great cedar gate of his city at night, lit by two torches, walls of sun-dried brick in deep shadow, and beyond them the river plain swallowed by a towering, creeping violet mist. Green light of the Time school rises from the paving stones below; violet mist from the right.

The hero belongs to the people of one face — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today, in a walled city of sun-dried brick on a green river plain, not far from the gates of Meshen-Gar. Subject: Nattu the Gate, a man of the people of one face, a defender of the Earth school. Who he is: he kept the gate of his city for thirty harvests, as his father's father had before him: everyone who entered named themselves and showed their face, and he looked whether it was the right face for the name. His shield was raw hide stretched over wood and never shone in any weather — the Many-Faced took the shape of those they touched the way water takes a reflection, but from his shield there was nothing to take. For three days and three nights he held the closed gate. Right now the tide of shifting shapes breaks against his shield. Character: steadfast, stern and weary — an old gatekeeper who does not open; his jaw set, his heavy brows lowered, his amber eyes unblinking; grey in his short beard. Pose, the moment of holding: the camera is low; he stands in the closed gate, turned toward the right, his shoulders driven forward. He has exactly two arms: his near arm drives a round shield of dull, matte raw hide forward toward the right, and a wave of violet mist full of half-formed faces breaks against it and slides off, unable to take any shape from it; his far hand grips the great wooden bar across the cedar gate behind him. Amber-orange light of the Earth school glows from the threshold stone below. Details that tell his story: (1) the shield is dull scraped hide with no shine at all; (2) behind him at the foot of the gate stand several bowls of dark clay filled with still water; (3) a heavy bronze gate key hangs at his belt on a thick cord; (4) his robe is plain, with a single dark band at the hem; (5) his near forearm is bare, with a faint grey smear where something touched it. Place: the inside of the city gate at night: walls of sun-dried brick, the great cedar gate bound with bronze, torchlight; violet mist seeping under the gate and through the cracks. Amber light from the threshold stone below; cold violet from the right.

Subject: Ziana Mirror-Water, a woman of the people of one face, a healer of the Water school. Who she is: still water tells the truth if nobody touches it — her people tested children and oaths that way. She kept bowls of dark clay filled to the brim and set in the shade; those whom the Many-Faced had touched, whose faces were melting like wax near a fire, she sat over a bowl, and the water showed them their own face, and it came back to them — not at once, over a night, line by line. The Many-Faced went around her bowls. Right now she holds out a bowl to a wounded one. Character: calm, compassionate and quietly fearless — a healer who has learned to fear familiar faces; her face serene, her eyes steady, her lips parted as she speaks softly. Pose, the moment of healing: the camera is low; she stands turned toward the right, leaning forward a little. She has exactly two arms: both hands hold out toward the right a wide, shallow bowl of dark clay filled to the brim with perfectly still water, which glows from within with clear blue light of the Water school; the calm light falls on the wounded beyond the right edge; the water is so still that it mirrors the sky. Details that tell her story: (1) behind her, rows of dark clay bowls filled to the brim stand in the shade; (2) her hands are steady — not a ripple on the water; (3) a single grey strand runs through her dark braid; (4) a plain robe with a single blue band at the hem; (5) a wet cloth over her shoulder. Place: a shaded courtyard inside the city walls at dusk: brick walls, a stone basin, and over the walls a violet mist creeping in from the fields. Blue light rises from the bowls below; violet mist from the right.

Subject: Eshmu Word-of-Form, a man of the people of one face, a battle mage of the Light school. Who he is: as a young man he went to Meshen-Gar to study — they knew more about form than anyone. Later he took the masks off a fallen priest — of bronze, clay, feathers, leather and wax, seven of them — and under the seventh there was nothing, smooth as an egg. For nine nights he searched for one word — the old name of everything at once, after which each thing remembers its own form — and on the tenth he found it. At the gates of Meshen-Gar he said it aloud, and the Many-Faced scattered like fog before the wind. Right now he speaks the word. Character: wise, grave and terrible in his certainty — an old scholar with no pity left; his head thrown back, his mouth open in the word, his amber eyes wide and shining with light. Pose, the moment of the word: the camera is low; he stands before tall gates, turned toward the right, his chest thrown forward. The hero belongs to the people of the red cliffs — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today, among cliffs and gorges of red sandstone at the edge of the desert, across the river from the kingdom of Ta-Nehem. Their enemies were the Undying of Ta-Nehem — the risen dead of a river kingdom of reeds and sand, dried with salt and wrapped in linen so that their form would not leave them, with gold masks, jackal-headed guards, chariots of bone and swarms of black beetles, who marched on the living to lead them into their eternal kingdom; dignified and eerie, never rotting; such things appear only as trophies or as the threat beyond the right edge.

When the Undying marched out of their tombs, their touch dried people like salt — the skin tightened, the legs went numb and walked by themselves after the wrapped dead; her balm gave the living back their warmth, and they stayed. Place: a stone well at the foot of the red cliffs at dusk: palm trees, the desert beyond, and from the right the long shadows of tall linen-wrapped figures stretching across the sand. Blue light of the Water school rises from the water in the well below.

The hero belongs to the people of the standing stones — a forgotten people who lived long before all the peoples of today, on windy moors of heather and mist. At birth each of them gets a stone in the circle with their name carved into it: while the name is on the stone, a person holds in the world like a boat on a rope. They look unlike any people living now: broad, strong and weathered, with square faces, strong brows, deep-set eyes of pale moss-green and wide straight mouths; their skin is pale with a faint cool grey tone, like lichen on stone, reddened by the wind; their hair is dark slate-grey streaked with silver even in the young, worn in heavy plaits. They wear cloaks of undyed wool in grey, brown and moss green pinned with bone pins, woollen tunics and leather belts; their tools are bronze chisels, wooden mallets, stone, rope and wooden rollers for raising stones. Their enemies were the Nameless — a people who gave up their names and went from circle to circle cutting the names off every stone: faceless stone-carriers, shadows with blank smooth shields and carvers with chisels, their faces smooth pale stone masks with no features, the hems of their grey cloaks fraying into mist; such things appear only as the threat beyond the right edge. A carved name is never shown as letters: it is only a deep shadowed hollow half-filled with moss, or it is hidden by light, by a hand or by flying stone chips.

Place: the stone circle on a moor at dusk, mist between the stones, heather, a small peat fire glowing warm. Amber light rises from the moss and the peat below.

Their enemies were the Nameless — a people who gave up their names and went from circle to circle cutting the names off every stone: faceless stone-carriers, shadows with blank smooth shields and carvers with chisels, their faces smooth pale stone masks with no features, the hems of their grey cloaks fraying into mist; such things appear only as the threat beyond the right edge. A carved name is never shown as letters: it is only a deep shadowed hollow half-filled with moss, or it is hidden by light, by a hand or by flying stone chips.

Subject: Menven Last-Name, a woman of the standing stones, a battle mage of the Time school. Who she is: the last of the people of the stones. She followed the old carver and learned to hold his chisel; when he laid it down, she carried it. Every winter she re-cut the names in her circle so that moss would not fill them — and once she understood that there would be no one to re-cut her own name after her, and she carved it anew, herself, deeper than before. Many winters later the last carver of the Nameless came to her stone, raised his chisel — and lowered it. Right now she stands before her stone and names the fallen aloud. Character: proud, sorrowful and unbreakable — the last one, who has nothing left to leave but a name; her head high, her mouth open as she calls the names, her moss-green eyes blazing with green light. Pose, the moment of the spell: the camera is low; she stands before her own tall standing stone, turned toward the right. She has exactly two arms: her near arm is raised toward the right, and in her hand the old black chisel points at the enemy like a wand — a torrent of green light of the Time school pours from it toward the Nameless beyond the right edge; her far palm is pressed flat against her stone, covering her carved name completely. Details that tell her story: (1) the black stone chisel, worn smooth, inherited from her master; (2) her palm on the stone hides the name entirely; (3) her plaits are more silver than grey, pinned with bone pins; (4) a cloak of undyed grey wool pinned at the shoulder with a bone pin; (5) around her the stones of her circle stand in a ring, green with moss — all the others are gone. Place: the last stone circle with names on a wide moor at night, mist, the smooth blank stones of other circles far away. Green light of the Time school rises from the ground below and flows from the chisel.

Who he is: the eldest son of an ordinary family in an ordinary land — work, hunger, brothers, everyone asleep in a heap by one stove. In the hungry winter, while his father and mother searched for food, he carried his little sister on his back through the snow and did not notice that she never grew heavier; he noticed later. Right now something moves in the blizzard beyond the right edge, and he stands between it and what he carries. Character: steady, simple, stubborn and gentle — an ordinary man who does not step back; his broad face set, his brows lowered against the wind, his grey eyes calm and fixed on the danger. A young man, broad-shouldered, with a short fair beard frosted with snow and a weathered, honest face. Amber-orange light of the Earth school bursts from cracks in the frozen ground below, and snow flies. Details that tell his story: (1) on his back a small bundle wrapped in an old patched sheepskin is tied with rope — light as a feather; (2) a peasant's coat of patched brown wool with a rope for a belt; (3) the cracked, calloused hands of a ploughman; (4) a heel of dark bread is tucked into his coat — he did not eat it; (5) snow crusted thick on his shoulders and hood. Place: a poor village of low houses in the hungry winter at dusk: snowdrifts, a single window glowing with the light of one stove, bare trees, a blizzard. Amber light rises from the frozen earth below; cold blue snow-light all around.

Subject: Aeris Bowstring, an elf of the great southern forest, a swift archer of the Air school. Who he is: he learned to shoot at the great Tree when the forest was young and the Tree did not yet reach the clouds — you could still shout to its top. The elves are monks with bows, and he was one of the best and knew it without pride; he was taught to shoot not at the beast but into the silence between two heartbeats. For two hundred years he stood on the southern edge of the forest. Right now, in that silence, he looses. Character: serene, precise and utterly calm — a master for whom the whole world stops; his face still, his eyes clear and focused, the faintest line between his brows. An elf with a long, fine face, long pointed ears, long pale hair tied back, grey-green eyes. Pose, the moment between two heartbeats: the camera is low; he stands at the edge of the forest, turned toward the right, the bow at full draw. He has exactly two arms: his near arm holds a tall longbow of pale living wood out toward the right; his far hand draws the string back to his cheek, the arrow aimed at the enemy beyond the right edge. Everything around him hangs still: falling leaves stop in mid-air, and a thin spiral of pale white-green wind of the Air school coils along the arrow. Details that tell his story: (1) the bow is of pale living wood with a few green leaves still growing on it; (2) a quiver of arrows fletched with white feathers; (3) a long grey-green cloak with the hood thrown back; (4) a thin braid with a single wooden bead behind his ear; (5) far behind him the great Tree rises above the young forest, its crown still below the clouds. Place: the southern edge of a young elven forest at dawn: slender young trees, clear light, the vast Tree in the distance. Pale white-green light of the Air school rises from the roots and moss below.

Subject: Hilda of the Dead Vein, a dwarf woman, a controller of the Dark school who cripples her foes. Who she is: a prospector who found veins by sound — a living vein rings, empty rock goes dull. Later she learned a darkness that puts out another's power — no fitting thing for a dwarf, and she took it. Right now she casts that darkness on an enemy. Subject: Beatrice, Smith of Bracelets, a woman of the great harbor city, a controller of the Water school. Who she is: for forty years she forged the bracelets of the bound debtors at the temple of the water god — a core of blue stone that binds, set in a band of green stone in which time does not pass. She set the core right over the pulse: the spell binds not the hand but what beats in the chest. The thickness is set by the debt, not by the smith. She swept the green dust from the floor by the forge and kept it in a pouch that glows in the dark. One day the order came to forge a bracelet for her own son. Right now she binds an enemy with a ring of blue light. Character: strong, exact and hard as her craft — a master who never asks why; grief held behind a stern face; her jaw set, her eyes focused. A powerful woman in her fifties with grey-streaked hair tied back, soot on her cheek and heavy forearms. Who she is: when all the peoples first stood together, she went with every elf who could hold a bow to the city at the middle of the world and was set on the wall by the gate. When the city rose into the sky, the wall rose with it, but the outer gate stayed on the ground, and she stayed at the gate. Her arrows ran out before the enemies did; a northerner brought her arrows carved from pale bone — they flew crooked, and she learned to shoot again. Right now she draws one of those crooked arrows. Details that tell her story: (1) a long pale bone hangs at her belt, covered along its length with tiny tally notches; (2) a quiver of crooked pale arrows; (3) a worn green cloak, torn and patched; (4) a scarred leather guard on her bow arm; (5) far above her, the city floating in the sky like a cloud. Who he is: at the start of the golden age everyone who had little and wanted much went down below, and he gathered forty — debtors, younger sons, two sister-weavers, an old herbwoman. These Faceless were once bound debtors of the great harbor city of the west — a city of white stone and red roofs built in terraces where a great river breaks into branches and falls to the sea; stone arches over its canals carry glowing blue stones in their keystones, and cypresses grow on its upper tiers. A bound debtor wore a bracelet: a core of blue stone set in a band of pale green stone. These five took it off, each through one of the narrow doors out of debt, and a pale band of skin remains on the wrist where it was. Subject: Celeste the Lamp, a woman of the city of mages, a battle mage of the Time school. Who she is: in the school of Time they learned to listen to stone that glows from within; in the shaft beneath the portal platform it lies along one vein, and the deeper, the purer — above the permitted depth it is cloudy like water after rain, below it is clear as glass in which light has frozen. She wanted to hear the purest stone just once; pure stone sounds like a string that has been touched and never let go. At night she went below the mark, and on the last ledge the stone shone so evenly that she left her lamp burning there to find her way back. Right now she draws the voice of the pure stone into a spell. Character: rapt, fearless and possessed — she has heard the note and cannot stop; her eyes half-closed as if listening, her lips parted, a look of bliss and resolve. A slim young woman with pale skin and long dark hair tied back, in a mage's gloves. Pose, the moment of the spell: the camera is low; she stands on the last narrow ledge deep in the shaft, turned toward the right. These Faceless were called into the Tower of Timelessness and stayed there: they know everything about the world and nothing about themselves. Subject: Liv, a bonesetter from the north of the first generation, one of the Faceless, a healer of the Light school. Who she is: in the first years wanderers in robes taught people with their hands; she had a well, and everyone who passed came to drink. Four of the wanderers were met with joy; the fifth, who carried a scythe, was met by no one — and once he stopped at her well and asked for water, and she poured it without spilling a drop. As an old woman she walked to the black Tower when it still stood on the bare ground at the crossroads of the world, and was called inside. The light she heals with now is not her own. Right now she offers a ladle of healing light. Character: kind, fearless and humble — the one who gives water to the one nobody welcomes; a warm, open gesture. Pose, the moment of healing: the camera is low; she stands by her well, turned toward the right. She has exactly two arms: her near hand holds out toward the right a wooden ladle full of water that shines with pale golden light of the Light school, and the light spills toward the wounded beyond the right edge without a single drop falling; her far hand rests on the well's rope, worn smooth and shiny. Details that tell her story: (1) a long woollen headscarf and shawl of undyed wool frame the smooth darkness where her face should be; (2) bundles of wooden splints and linen strips at her belt — a bonesetter's tools; (3) old, strong hands; (4) a wooden bucket on the rim of the well; (5) far behind her, at a dusty crossroads, a black Tower rises straight from the bare ground. Place: an old stone well at a crossroads of the first age at dusk: dust, stones, tracks in four directions and none toward the Tower. Pale golden light from the ladle; green time-light rising from below.

Who he is: the best fighter of the first generation, taught by a wanderer-god himself — the teacher did not explain, he struck until you understood. His axe reached his shoulder and could not be held in one hand; it was the first of its kind. His fear never left him — it stood beside him like a second man in the line, and he learned to fight shoulder to shoulder with it. On a beach of pale sand by a cold sea, long before any arena existed, he went out against his teacher knowing he would lose, and lost standing to the last blow. Right now he swings the first axe. Character: fierce, afraid and unstoppable — courage that walks side by side with fear; a huge, scarred warrior. Pose, the moment of the blow: the camera is low; he strides toward the right across the sand, his torso twisted, his shoulders rolled back. He has exactly two arms: both hands swing a great two-handed axe from high over his far shoulder down toward the right in one tremendous blow; the broad bronze head, large and close to the camera near the top of the picture, trails scarlet fire of the Fire school. Details that tell his story: (1) a heavy hood of rough brown wool frames the smooth darkness where his face should be; (2) both hands are thick with calluses, the knuckles scarred; (3) a scarlet light burns in the middle of his chest through his leather jerkin, rising up to his throat — the mark of the god's gaze; (4) his long shadow on the sand stretches beside him like a second warrior in the line; (5) the cold sea foams on the sand behind him. Place: a wide beach of fine pale sand by a cold grey sea at dusk in the first age: no walls, no benches, only footprints washed by the tide. Scarlet light from the axe and from glowing cracks in the wet sand below; green time-sand drifts around him.

Details that tell his story: (1) a hood of undyed wool frames the smooth darkness where his face should be; (2) a blue light burns in the middle of his chest through his clothing, brimming over like a vessel under a stream — the mark of the god's gaze; (3) a leather water-skin at his belt; (4) the rim of the shield is worn smooth; (5) behind him, large plain stones stand by the water — no marks on them. Place: the bank where a great river breaks into branches and falls to the sea, in the first age, at dusk: large plain stones, rushing water, no houses at all. Subject: Gisla the Swift, a dwarf woman of the first generation, one of the Faceless, a swift fighter of the Earth school. Character: quick, sharp and restless — a mind that is always a step ahead; she is short and broad, but light and fast. Pose, the moment of the strike: the camera is low; she darts forward toward the right, low and fast, her body twisting into the blow. Chips of stone fly. Details that tell her story: (1) a leather hood, and two thick braids that fall from the smooth darkness where her face should be, bound with copper rings — no beard; (2) an amber light burns in the middle of her chest, filling it like a mine filling with water — the mark of the god's gaze; (3) her knuckles are scarred from knocking on stone to listen to it; (4) a miner's leather jerkin and a belt of small pouches of ore; (5) a glowing amber vein in the rock wall behind her. Place: the first mine of the dwarves in the first age: a fresh tunnel of raw rock, a single amber vein shining. Amber light rises from the vein and the cracks below; green time-sand drifts around her.

The hero's body is turned toward the right side of the picture, toward unseen enemies beyond the right edge. Rich atmospheric background that tells where the hero lived, with depth and soft focus, darker than the character. Light comes from below; rim light separates the figure from the background.

This hero is one of the Faceless: a soul of the distant past whose face has long been worn away, and who does not remember who they were. Where the face should be, inside the hood or head-covering, there is only a smooth, soft, deep darkness, as dark as a night sky — no pale surface, no smooth mask, no eye holes, no eyes, no glowing eyes, no nose, no mouth, no skull, no features at all in that darkness; the face is rubbed away like the face of an old coin. Everything else about the hero is vivid and specific: the clothing, the silhouette, the weapon and above all the hands — alive, strong and expressive. Fine green sand of time drifts from the edges of the cloak and from the fingertips and floats upward — the mark of the timeless. The rarity is the highest in the game: the portrait feels precious and regal, with old gold highlights and deep green light.

These are the Marked — the best fighters of the first generation, in the young world of the first age, when the gods walked the land as wanderers in robes and taught people with their hands. Each of them was once looked upon by their own god, and that gaze was more than a person can hold. The god is never shown. The mark of the gaze: in the middle of the hero's chest a light burns in the colour of their school, as if the hourglass of their heart were filled to overflowing; it glows through the clothing. This set is the summit of the showcase: the most magnificent, heroic and dangerous of all the Faceless — legends at the moment of their greatest deed, with the richest light and the boldest pose.

Subject: Yalen, a man of the first generation, one of the Faceless, a battle mage of the Time school. Who he is: the best mage of his generation in the school of Time, when it still asked nothing in return — it took from what flows past anyway, held it for a moment and let it go. He could hear other people's hourglasses: the children's quick, the old ones' slow like drips after rain, the sick ones' stumbling; he knew whose sand was running out before they did, and never said so. Right now he stops the sand of an enemy. Character: quiet, watchful and burdened by silence — the child who watched the grown-ups too carefully, grown into a master. Pose, the moment of the spell: the camera is low; he stands turned toward the right. He has exactly two arms: his near hand is raised toward the right, the fingers slowly closing, and around the enemy beyond the right edge the streaming green sand of time halts in mid-air; his far hand is held open at his side, and around him float many small, ghostly hourglasses of green light, each running at its own pace. Details that tell his story: (1) a deep hood of dark green wool frames the smooth darkness where his face should be; (2) a green light burns in the middle of his chest, and the sand in it stands still — the mark of the god's gaze; (3) a simple robe of the first school, without ornament; (4) his fingers are long and perfectly still; (5) some of the ghostly hourglasses around him are nearly empty. Place: a simple stone courtyard of the first school of Time at dusk in the first age: a few pillars, an open sky, sand drifting upward. Green time-light rises from below and from the hourglasses.

The player must feel the difference in power at a glance, before reading any number: from left to right the frame grows richer, the light brighter, the aura and the particles stronger. Each card may spill its glow and particles onto the dark background around it.

They give the exact look of these elements on the cards; do not copy their plain square backgrounds.

The hero, the same on all three cards: the old dwarf from image 1 — a bald head, a stern furrowed face, a long white braided beard, a heavy brown leather coat studded with iron rivets, a round iron-rimmed shield on his arm, a heavy chain with a huge old iron key across his chest. Keep his face, clothes, colors and pose as in image 1. He is painted edge to edge inside the card's window: head in the upper third, shown down to the hips; the dark stone and amber crystals of his portrait fill the window behind him.

Card anatomy — the same on all three cards and in the same places, unless the concept below says otherwise:
- Top center: the rarity crystal from images 2–4, set into the top of the frame: white on the left card, violet on the middle card, green on the right card. One crystal per card.
- Just below the crystal, along the top edge of the window: valor stars in a short arc — small solid four-pointed stars like the star in image 7, without its tile: each star has exactly four long sharp rays, pointing up, down, left and right, like a compass star — never a five-pointed star. The number of star places is the hero's personal maximum. Left card: one place, empty — a dark hollow socket. Middle card: three places — two filled with glowing gold, one empty socket. Right card: five places, all five filled and blazing gold.

- Exactly five small rune stones like images 5 and 6 — five in total, never six: a column of three on the left side of the portrait and a shorter column of only two on the right side. Left card: all five unlit, dark grey. Middle card: the three on the left lit with turquoise light inside, the two on the right unlit. Right card: all five lit.
- Bottom: a blank name plaque across the card — smooth, with nothing written on it. Under it one row: the class icon from image 9 (a shield on a hexagonal tile) on the left, and the combat power — the crossed-swords icon from image 8 followed by the number — to its right: 1240 on the left card, 48350 on the middle card, 912780 on the right card.
The digits are clean, bold and legible, in light warm gold.

Left card: a plain narrow frame of dull dark bronze with flat edges and no ornament; plain bronze bezels hold the crystal, the star socket and the rune stones; no glow at all, the portrait slightly muted. Right card: a sumptuous frame of polished old gold with dense openwork filigree along every edge; a tall crest with spread golden wings and rays around a large green crystal; the corners grow into ornate gold flourishes set with small green gems; a warm golden radiance blazes behind the whole card and spills onto the background; embers and bright gold sparks swirl around the card; a short ribbon of plain crimson silk, with nothing written on it, is draped across the top right corner as the sign of the maximum.

Subject: the Workshop of Forms (air, the god Vial), the first hall under Endalor. The place: a hall so huge that its vault is lost in darkness and its walls in haze; here the god once sculpted living beings from clay before giving them to the world above, and the work was left in the middle. Bodies come out of the walls half-sculpted — an arm without a hand, a back without a face, a beast with only one half made. Heavy wooden worktables stand in rows with unfinished clay works, sculpting chisels and clay-stained cloths. Pale sand is everywhere: it lies in drifts between the tables, falls from cracks in the vault in thin streams, and in places stands as a column of falling sand from floor to vault, like an hourglass no one turns. Light: white-green crystals grow in the cracks of the floor and walls and glow from within, like a candle left in each, and throw a cold halo upward; the only warm color in the hall is the ochre clay. The silence of a workshop abandoned in the middle of the day. Nothing is ugly: every body is made precisely and calmly, just not finished. Who waits here, from near to far: (1) in the middle distance, between the worktables, never in the foreground and each no taller than a quarter of the picture, three unfinished elves of grey-green clay stand turned toward the viewer — the Faceless one, a slender elf-shaped figure in a sketch of clothing with a rope for a belt, holding a stone blank of a sword without a guard; his smooth face has only two shallow thumb marks where the eyes should be, and still he looks straight at you; the Long-armed one, thin and stooped, whose one arm reaches almost to the floor and ends in a heavy stone hand; the Hollow one, whose chest is open like an empty mold, his head thrown back, a thin whirl of sand and air leaving his chest; (2) at a table in the middle distance on the right, two servants in clay aprons who still keep working — a thickset apprentice with forearms twice as thick as they should be, kneading a lump of clay, and a tall stooped carver whose right hand is a fan of thin blades — both have raised their heads and look at the viewer; (3) far in the depth, towering over the last tables, the First Sketch — a hunched giant three times the height of a man, so even far away he stands three times taller than the elves near the viewer and his head reaches the haze under the vault, made of two halves that do not match: the left half an elf, the right half a beast with clay fur, a clawed paw and a beast's leg; instead of a face a smooth mask with two hollows; a small foreign hand is stuck on his side; he is trying a clay part against his own body; (4) at the very end of the hall, in front of a tall dark passage that glows faintly white-green and leads deeper down, stands the Master — the only finished one: a tall slender elf of smooth polished clay with long hair and a calm face, eyes closed, a master's apron, wrapped forearms, a chisel of glowing white-green stone at his belt, one hand raised palm forward: stop. He is small with distance but clearly readable against the light of the passage. Composition: the path between the worktables leads from the bottom of the picture to the Master and the glowing passage; the First Sketch looms in the haze just before it; columns of falling sand stand on both sides of the path; the left quarter is the near wall of the hall in deep shadow — no figure stands there, only the faint relief of a half-sculpted body in the stone; the upper left is dark vault; the bottom of the picture is dark floor with drifts of sand, empty of figures.

No gore, no blood, no skulls, no bones, no corpses, no undead, no twisted or distorted creatures, no demons. No purple, no violet, no magenta light. No heroes, no adventurers, no people from the surface world — only the inhabitants of this place. Composition: the viewer stands at the top of the stairs into the hall; the rows of stacks recede to the Keeper and the Seer; the left quarter is a near stack in deep shadow; the upper left is dark vault; the bottom of the picture is dark stone floor.

Format: a concept sheet for the hero card of a dark fantasy mobile RPG, landscape 16:9. On a plain dark background — near-black slate (#0C0E11) with a soft vignette, no table, no scenery — stand exactly three vertical hero cards side by side in one row, evenly spaced and the same size. Each card is tall and narrow, in a 9:16 proportion, about five sixths of the canvas high, seen straight on, flat, not tilted, not in perspective, fully inside the canvas with a small margin. The three cards show the same hero with the same card design at three steps of power, from left to right: weak, strong, legendary. The frame grows richer from left to right, and the icons on the card tell the player exactly how strong the hero is. This sheet presents one system of icons: the layout is the same on all three cards, only the states of the icons and the richness of the frame change. Every icon must be easy to read and to count.

The first attached image is the hero's portrait: the old dwarf — a bald head, a stern furrowed face, a long white braided beard, a heavy brown leather coat studded with iron rivets, a round iron-rimmed shield on his arm, a heavy chain with a huge old iron key across his chest. Paint him the same on all three cards, with his face, clothes, colors and pose as in the portrait, edge to edge inside the card's window, head in the upper third, shown down to the hips. The other attached images are our game icons, listed in the concept below; they give the exact look of these elements on the cards; do not copy their plain square backgrounds.

What the three cards must show — the concept below says how:
- rarity: the left card is common — white (#E6E8EA); the middle card is epic — violet (#A986EE); the right card is timeless — green (#5FD67A);
- valor — the hero's personal maximum and how much of it is taken: left — maximum 1, taken 0; middle — maximum 3, taken 2; right — maximum 5, taken 5. There are exactly as many valor places as the maximum, never more;
- rune limits — always exactly five places: left — none passed; middle — three passed; right — all five passed;
- level: 34, 512, 1200; combat power: 1240, 48350, 912780 — digits only, never with a word or letters: the combat power is always the crossed-swords icon standing right before its number, with no letters such as CP or BP;
- class: tank — the shield icon; element: Earth — a small round medallion of dark iron and old gold around a chunk of amber rock glowing from within (#EB9D40).
Every card also has a blank name plaque with nothing written on it. The digits are clean, bold and legible, in light warm gold.

Concept: All Gems — every sign on the card is a stone set into the iron. Attached icons after the portrait: (2) the rarity crystal; (3) a lit rune stone; (4) an unlit rune stone; (5) the combat power icon — crossed swords; (6) the class icon — a shield on a hexagonal tile.

Frame — forged iron and gold. Left card: rough black iron straps with plain round rivets, a patch of rust, cold light. Middle card: the iron is inlaid with lines of gold, the seams glow faintly orange. Right card: a massive frame of dark iron with thick gold inlay and gold-capped rivets, the seams glow red-hot, embers and sparks fly up, molten light drips at the bottom.

Icons and layout:
- Rarity: one large rarity crystal (image 2) in the crest at the top center — white, violet, green.
- Rune limits: five rune stones (images 3 and 4) set one above another down the left rail of the frame. Left card: all five unlit. Middle card: the upper three lit with turquoise light, the lower two unlit. Right card: all five lit.
- Valor: claw settings down the right rail of the frame from the top, as many as the valor maximum. A taken valor is a faceted gold gem shining like a small sun; an empty place is an empty dark claw setting. Left card: one single empty claw setting at the top of the right rail, and the rest of the rail is plain iron. Middle card: three settings — the top two hold shining gold gems, the third is empty, the rest of the rail plain. Right card: five shining gold gems down the whole right rail.
- Level: the level number on a round iron boss at the top left corner of the frame.
- Bottom corners: the class icon (image 6) set like a cameo in the bottom left corner, the element medallion in the bottom right corner.
- Between them at the bottom: the blank name plaque and under it the combat power — the crossed swords (image 5) and the number.

No words, no letters, no real-world alphabets, no Roman numerals, no runes, glyphs or markings that look like writing, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no captions, titles or labels above or under the cards. The only characters anywhere in the picture are the digits of the level and combat power numbers — no word Level, no Lv, no abbreviations such as CP, BP or PWR, no letters on any badge or plate; the name plaque stays blank. No pentagrams, no occult signs, no crosses. No phone mockup, no hands holding the cards, no table, no perspective, no tilted or overlapping cards, no fourth card. The hero has exactly two arms and two hands; no empty eyes.

This sheet presents one system of icons: the layout is the same on all three cards, only the states of the icons and the richness of the frame change. Every icon must be easy to read and to count.

The first attached image is the hero's portrait: the old dwarf — a bald head, a stern furrowed face, a long white braided beard, a heavy brown leather coat studded with iron rivets, a round iron-rimmed shield on his arm, a heavy chain with a huge old iron key across his chest. Paint him the same on all three cards, with his face, clothes, colors and pose as in the portrait, edge to edge inside the card's window, head in the upper third, shown down to the hips. The other attached images are our game icons, listed in the concept below; they give the exact look of these elements on the cards; do not copy their plain square backgrounds.

What the three cards must show — the concept below says how:
- rarity: the left card is common — white (#E6E8EA); the middle card is epic — violet (#A986EE); the right card is timeless — green (#5FD67A);

- rune limits — always exactly five places: left — none passed; middle — three passed; right — all five passed;
- level: 34, 512, 1200; combat power: 1240, 48350, 912780 — digits only, never with a word or letters: the combat power is always the crossed-swords icon standing right before its number, with no letters such as CP or BP;
- class: tank — the shield icon; element: Earth — a small round medallion of dark iron and old gold around a chunk of amber rock glowing from within (#EB9D40).
Every card also has a blank name plaque with nothing written on it. The digits are clean, bold and legible, in light warm gold.

Concept: the Sash and the Blade. Attached icons after the portrait: (2) the rarity crystal; (3) the combat power icon — crossed swords; (4) the class icon — a shield on a hexagonal tile.

Frame — forged iron and gold. Left card: rough black iron straps with plain round rivets, a patch of rust, cold light. Middle card: the iron is inlaid with lines of gold, the seams glow faintly orange. Right card: a massive frame of dark iron with thick gold inlay and gold-capped rivets, the seams glow red-hot, embers and sparks fly up.

Icons and layout:
- Rune limits: a straight sword runs down the whole left edge of the card as part of the frame, its hilt at the top left, its blade pointing down. The blade has five notches along it, evenly spaced. A passed limit is a notch glowing turquoise; an unpassed one is a dark notch. Left card: all five dark. Middle card: the upper three glow, the lower two are dark. Right card: all five glow.
- Rarity: the rarity crystal (image 2) set in the sword's pommel at the top left — white, violet, green — and the sash below has the same color.
- The sash: a broad band of heavy cloth runs diagonally across the lower half of the card, from the right edge down to the bottom left, over the hero's coat, like an order's ribbon, in the rarity color: grey-white, violet, green. The combat power is on the sash in gold: the crossed swords (image 3) and the number.
- Valor: medals pinned to the sash above the number, in a row along it, as many places as the valor maximum. A taken valor is a round gold medal with a four-pointed star; an empty place is a small empty dark ring. Left card: one single empty ring and nothing more. Middle card: three places — the first two are gold medals, the third is an empty ring. Right card: five gold medals.
- Top right corner: a round badge with the level number; under it the element medallion. Bottom right corner: the class icon (image 4).
- The blank name plaque runs across the top of the card, to the right of the sword's hilt.

No words, no letters, no real-world alphabets, no Roman numerals, no runes, glyphs or markings that look like writing, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no captions, titles or labels above or under the cards. Art style: dark fantasy game art for a mobile RPG — gloomy, heavy, noble and uneasy. Hand-painted digital painting, the same painting as the attached hero portrait: visible confident brush strokes, simplified planes, deep near-black shadows, crisp rim light on edges. A muted, desaturated palette: soot black (#050607, #121518), graphite (#262B31), old blackened iron, yellowed bone, dark wood, weathered stone, tarnished dark bronze. Everything is matte, worn and aged: no bright or polished gold, no gloss, no shiny jewellery, no clean saturated game-UI colors. Light is scarce and precious: the scene is lit only from below — cold turquoise carst light (#48E5D4) rising from cracks and crystals — while the stones, flames and signs on the card glow on their own; everything else sinks into shadow. Ash, dust motes and faint embers drift in the light. A hero's power shows as awe and dread, not as wealth. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime, no cartoon, no flat vector style.

Draw exactly one image in a single pass: no alternative versions, no second attempts, no text in the reply.

Format: a concept sheet for the hero card of a dark fantasy mobile RPG, landscape 16:9. In deep darkness — a near-black background (#050607) with a little drifting ash and a faint cold turquoise glow rising from below the bottom edge; no table, no floor, no scenery — stand exactly three vertical hero cards side by side in one row, evenly spaced and the same size. Each card is tall and narrow, in a 9:16 proportion, about four fifths of the canvas high, seen straight on, flat, not tilted, not in perspective, fully inside the canvas with a margin. The three cards show the same hero with the same card design at three steps of power, from left to right: weak, strong, legendary. From left to right the card grows from humble and dim to ancient and awe-inspiring: the frame becomes heavier and more elaborate, the light from below stronger, the ash and embers denser. This sheet presents one system of icons: the layout is the same on all three cards, only the states of the icons and the weight of the frame change. The icons glow on their own and stay easy to read and to count even in the dark.

The first attached image is the hero's portrait: the old dwarf — a bald head, a stern furrowed face, a long white braided beard, a heavy brown leather coat studded with iron rivets, a round iron-rimmed shield on his arm, a heavy chain with a huge old iron key across his chest. Paint him the same on all three cards, with his face, clothes and pose as in the portrait, inside the card's window, head in the upper third, shown down to the hips — but in the dark key of the card: the background behind him sinks into deep shadow — no pale sky, no snow, no bright background — and the light comes from below, catching his beard, face and shield. The other attached images are our game icons, listed in the concept below; they give the shape of these elements on the cards; paint them in the same dark, matte, aged key as the card, and do not copy their plain square backgrounds.

What the three cards must show — the concept below says how:
- rarity: the left card is common — white (#E6E8EA); the middle card is epic — violet (#A986EE); the right card is timeless — green (#5FD67A);
- valor — the hero's personal maximum and how much of it is taken: left — maximum 1, taken 0; middle — maximum 3, taken 2; right — maximum 5, taken 5. There are exactly as many valor places as the maximum, never more;
- rune limits — always exactly five places: left — none passed; middle — three passed; right — all five passed;
- level: 34, 512, 1200; combat power: 1240, 48350, 912780 — digits only, never with a word or letters: the combat power is always the crossed-swords icon standing right before its number, with no letters such as CP or BP;
- class: tank — the shield icon; element: a small round medallion of dark iron around a raw chunk of amber-orange rock glowing from within (#EB9D40) — a rock, not a planet: no globe, no map, no continents.
Every card also has a blank name plaque with nothing written on it. The digits are clean, bold and legible, in pale old gold or bone color.

Concept: the Bone Reliquary — the card is a narrow shrine that keeps the hero like a relic. Attached icons after the portrait: (2) the rarity crystal; (3) a lit rune stone; (4) an unlit rune stone; (5) the combat power icon — crossed swords; (6) the class icon — a shield on a hexagonal tile.

Frame — carved old yellowed bone and dark wood bound with blackened iron. No skulls, no skeletons, no bones of a body: the bone is carved into plain ribs, knots and tracery. Left card: a plain narrow frame of dark worn wood with thin strips of yellowed bone, cracked and sooty, a few iron nails; dim. Middle card: the wood is inlaid with carved bone ribs along both sides, a small pointed bone gable over the window, blackened iron bands; warm candle light. Right card: a tall ancient reliquary — a pointed arch of carved bone tracery over the window, slender bone spires on both sides, heavy blackened iron bands; light pours up from below, ash and embers rise; solemn and awe-inspiring.

Every card carries the same eight signs in the same places — the left card too:
1) at the very top of the frame, the rarity crystal (image 2) in a blackened iron claw setting;
2) right under it, a narrow bone shelf along the top edge of the window with a row of candles — the valor;
3) in the top left corner, a small bone tag with the level digits;
4) in the top right corner, the element medallion;
5) across the bottom of the window, a straight row of exactly five small blackened iron cages, each holding one rune stone like images 3 and 4 — the rune limits; the stones are plain, with no letters, runes or signs on them, only a small diamond-shaped spark at the center of a lit one;
6) under the cages, a blank bone name plaque;
7) under the plaque, on the left, the class icon (image 6);
8) next to it, on the right, the crossed swords (image 5) followed by the combat power number.

What differs from card to card:
- Left card: a milky-white crystal; one single candle on the shelf, unlit, with a black wick — nothing more on the shelf; level 34; all five cage stones dull grey; combat power 1240.
- Middle card: a violet crystal (#A986EE); exactly three candles — the left and the middle burn with violet flames, the right one is unlit; level 512; the three cage stones on the left glow turquoise, the two on the right are dull; combat power 48350.
- Right card: a green crystal (#5FD67A) — a crystal, not a rune stone; five candles, all burning with green flames, wax dripping over the shelf; level 1200; all five cage stones glow turquoise and their light rises onto the hero; combat power 912780.

No words, no letters, no real-world alphabets, no Roman numerals, no runes, glyphs or markings that look like writing, no lines of text on pages, leather or stone, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no captions, titles or labels above or under the cards. The only characters anywhere in the picture are the digits of the level and combat power numbers — no word Level, no Lv, no abbreviations such as CP, BP or PWR, no letters on any badge or plate; the name plaque stays blank. No skulls, no skeletons, no blood, no gore. No pentagrams, no occult signs, no crosses, no religious symbols. No bright polished gold, no glossy plastic shine, no clean bright mobile-game UI look. No phone mockup, no hands holding the cards, no table, no floor, no perspective, no tilted or overlapping cards, no fourth card. The hero has exactly two arms and two hands; no empty eyes.

A muted, desaturated palette: soot black (#050607, #121518), graphite (#262B31), old blackened iron, yellowed bone, dark wood, weathered stone, tarnished dark bronze. Everything is matte, worn and aged: no bright or polished gold, no gloss, no shiny jewellery, no clean saturated game-UI colors. Light is scarce and precious: the scene is lit only from below — cold turquoise carst light (#48E5D4) rising from cracks and crystals — while the stones, flames and signs on the card glow on their own; everything else sinks into shadow. Ash, dust motes and faint embers drift in the light. A hero's power shows as awe and dread, not as wealth. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime, no cartoon, no flat vector style.

Draw exactly one image in a single pass: no alternative versions, no second attempts, no text in the reply.

Format: a concept sheet for the hero card of a dark fantasy mobile RPG, landscape 16:9. In deep darkness — a near-black background (#050607) with a little drifting ash and a faint cold turquoise glow rising from below the bottom edge; no table, no floor, no scenery — stand exactly three vertical hero cards side by side in one row, evenly spaced and the same size. Each card is tall and narrow, in a 9:16 proportion, about four fifths of the canvas high, seen straight on, flat, not tilted, not in perspective, fully inside the canvas with a margin. The three cards show the same hero with the same card design at three steps of power, from left to right: weak, strong, legendary. From left to right the card grows from humble and dim to ancient and awe-inspiring: the frame becomes heavier and more elaborate, the light from below stronger, the ash and embers denser. This sheet presents one system of icons: the layout is the same on all three cards, only the states of the icons and the weight of the frame change. The icons glow on their own and stay easy to read and to count even in the dark.

The first attached image is the hero's portrait: the old dwarf — a bald head, a stern furrowed face, a long white braided beard, a heavy brown leather coat studded with iron rivets, a round iron-rimmed shield on his arm, a heavy chain with a huge old iron key across his chest. Paint him the same on all three cards, with his face, clothes and pose as in the portrait, inside the card's window, head in the upper third, shown down to the hips — but in the dark key of the card: the background behind him sinks into deep shadow — no pale sky, no snow, no bright background — and the light comes from below, catching his beard, face and shield. The other attached images are our game icons, listed in the concept below; they give the shape of these elements on the cards; paint them in the same dark, matte, aged key as the card, and do not copy their plain square backgrounds.

What the three cards must show — the concept below says how:
- rarity: the left card is common — white (#E6E8EA); the middle card is epic — violet (#A986EE); the right card is timeless — green (#5FD67A);
- valor — the hero's personal maximum and how much of it is taken: left — maximum 1, taken 0; middle — maximum 3, taken 2; right — maximum 5, taken 5. There are exactly as many valor places as the maximum, never more;
- rune limits — always exactly five places: left — none passed; middle — three passed; right — all five passed;
- level: 34, 512, 1200; combat power: 1240, 48350, 912780 — digits only, never with a word or letters: the combat power is always the crossed-swords icon standing right before its number, with no letters such as CP or BP;
- class: tank — the shield icon; element: a small round medallion of dark iron around a raw chunk of amber-orange rock glowing from within (#EB9D40) — a rock, not a planet: no globe, no map, no continents.
Every card also has a blank name plaque with nothing written on it. The digits are clean, bold and legible, in pale old gold or bone color.

Concept: the Grimoire — the card is the front cover of an ancient heavy tome: dark scorched leather over wooden boards, iron corners and locks; the hero's portrait is a painted panel set into the cover. No pages are open and nothing is written anywhere: no letters, no lines of text, no symbols on the leather. Attached icons after the portrait: (2) the rarity crystal; (3) the combat power icon — crossed swords; (4) the class icon — a shield on a hexagonal tile.

Frame. Left card: a worn plain cover of cracked brown leather with frayed, scorched edges and four small rusty iron corners. Middle card: tooled dark leather with a blind-stamped border of simple knots, blackened iron corners with rivets, a faint violet glow leaking from the page edges along the right side of the book. Right card: a massive cover bound in blackened iron and old bone, heavy iron corners with thorns, the page edges blaze with green light that spills out between the boards; ash and sparks rise; the book feels dangerous and alive.

Icons and layout:
- Rarity: the rarity crystal (image 2) set in an iron boss at the top center of the cover — white, violet, green — and the light leaking from the page edges has the same color.
- Rune limits: five small iron padlocks in one vertical column down the right edge of the cover, each with a keyhole, holding the book shut. A passed limit is an unlocked open padlock with turquoise light streaming out of its keyhole; an unpassed one is a closed dark padlock. Left card: all five closed and dark. Middle card: the upper three open and shining, the lower two closed. Right card: all five open, light streaming.
- Valor: wax seals hanging on short cords from the bottom edge of the cover, dangling just below the card like the seals of an old charter — as many cords as the valor maximum. A taken valor is a round seal of dark red wax impressed with a star; an empty place is a bare cord ending in an empty dark iron ring, with no wax. Left card: one single cord with an empty ring and nothing more. Middle card: exactly three cords — the left and the middle carry red wax seals, the right one ends in an empty ring. Right card: five cords, all with red wax seals.
- Level: digits tooled into a small round leather roundel at the top left corner. Element: the element medallion as an iron boss at the top right corner.
- Bottom of the cover: a blank dark metal name plate; under it one row: the class icon (image 4) on the left and the combat power — the crossed swords (image 3) and the number — on the right.

No words, no letters, no real-world alphabets, no Roman numerals, no runes, glyphs or markings that look like writing, no lines of text on pages, leather or stone, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no captions, titles or labels above or under the cards. The only characters anywhere in the picture are the digits of the level and combat power numbers — no word Level, no Lv, no abbreviations such as CP, BP or PWR, no letters on any badge or plate; the name plaque stays blank. No skulls, no skeletons, no blood, no gore. No pentagrams, no occult signs, no crosses, no religious symbols. No bright polished gold, no glossy plastic shine, no clean bright mobile-game UI look. No phone mockup, no hands holding the cards, no table, no floor, no perspective, no tilted or overlapping cards, no fourth card. The hero has exactly two arms and two hands; no empty eyes.

Промт, как он ушёл в модель
Art style: dark fantasy game art for a mobile RPG — gloomy, heavy, noble and uneasy. Hand-painted digital painting, the same painting as the attached samples: visible confident brush strokes, simplified planes, deep near-black shadows, crisp rim light on edges. A muted, desaturated palette: soot black (#050607, #121518), graphite (#262B31), old leather, blackened iron, dark bronze, yellowed bone, aged parchment. Everything is matte, worn and aged: no bright or polished gold, no gloss, no shiny jewellery, no clean saturated game-UI colors. Light is scarce and precious: the scene is lit only from below — cold turquoise carst light (#48E5D4) — while the crystals, padlocks, page edges and valor signs glow on their own; everything else sinks into shadow. Ash, dust motes and faint embers drift in the light. A hero's power shows as awe and age, not as wealth. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime, no cartoon, no flat vector style.

Draw exactly one image in a single pass: no alternative versions, no second attempts, no text in the reply.

This is a concept for the hero cards of a dark fantasy mobile RPG in which every hero is a book: tapping the card opens the book, and everything about the hero — skills, growth, the chapters of his story — is a part of that book. The first attached image is the hero's portrait. The second attached image is the approved style sample: take from it the dark painted book covers, the column of five padlocks with their turquoise light, the round level badge, the element medallion, the class shield, the combat power icon and the glow around the book — but none of its red wax seals, cords or rings: there are no wax seals anywhere. The other attached images are our game icons, listed below; they give the shape of these elements; paint them in the same dark, matte, aged key, and do not copy their plain square backgrounds.

The rules of the book system:
- The kind of book is the hero's personal valor maximum, from 1 to 5. The book grows in mass, craft and age, never in gloss: 1 — a small plain book in soft worn brown leather over thin boards, no metal at all; 2 — a sturdier book in dark leather with four iron corner pieces and one leather strap with an iron buckle across its lower part; 3 — a tome in an oklad: the cover framed by plates of dark bronze with engraved borders and bronze bosses at the corners; 4 — a heavy codex: thick boards in black leather bound with iron straps, plates of carved yellowed bone at the corners, large iron bosses; 5 — a grimoire: a massive cover in a rich oklad of blackened iron and carved bone with spiked iron corners, its page edges blazing with light that spills out, ash and embers rising.
- Rarity is the crystal set at the top center of the book plus the color of the glow around the book: common — white (#E6E8EA), almost no glow; rare — yellow (#F0CC4F); unique — turquoise (#1FB8D0); epic — violet (#A986EE); timeless — green (#5FD67A).
- Rune limits are always exactly five small iron padlocks hanging in one vertical column along the right edge of the book. A passed limit is an open padlock, unlocked, with turquoise light (#48E5D4) streaming out of its keyhole; an unpassed one is a closed dark padlock. Passed limits count from the top.
- Valor: the book has exactly as many valor places as its maximum, never more; the concept below says what they look like. A valor sign never looks like a padlock or a crystal.
- Level: digits in a round badge at the top left. Element: a small round medallion of dark iron around a raw chunk of amber-orange rock glowing from within (#EB9D40) — a rock, not a planet — at the top right. Class: the tank's shield icon at the bottom left. Combat power: the crossed-swords icon right before its number, at the bottom right. Digits only — never a word, never letters such as Lv, CP or BP. The digits are clean, bold and legible, in pale old gold.
- The hero, wherever he is painted: the old dwarf of the first attached image — a bald head, a stern furrowed face, a long white braided beard, a heavy brown leather coat studded with iron rivets, a round iron-rimmed shield, a heavy chain with a huge old iron key — the same face, clothes and pose, head in the upper third, shown down to the hips, his background in deep shadow, lit from below; his beard stays white. Under his portrait, a blank name plate with nothing written on it.

Format: a concept sheet, landscape 21:9. On near-black darkness with a faint turquoise glow rising from below — no table, no floor, no scenery — stand exactly five closed books side by side in one row, each seen straight on from the front as a vertical card in a 9:16 proportion, about two thirds of the canvas high, evenly spaced, the same size, flat, not tilted, not in perspective, placed a little above the middle so that the ribbons hanging below them fit in the canvas. From left to right they are the five kinds of book, 1 to 5, with the hero's portrait painted on a panel set into each cover. Attached icons after the style sample: (3) the white crystal — common; (4) the yellow crystal — rare; (5) the turquoise crystal — unique; (6) the violet crystal — epic; (7) the green crystal — timeless; (8) the combat power icon — crossed swords; (9) the class icon — a shield on a hexagonal tile.

Valor in this concept — bookmark ribbons, the chapters of his story that the hero has opened. Flat silk bookmark ribbons hang out of the bottom edge of the book, from under the name plate, and dangle below the book side by side — as many ribbons as the book's valor maximum. A taken valor is a ribbon of the book's rarity color ending in a small metal four-pointed star that glows amber-gold (#E6A84B); an untaken one is a faded, frayed grey ribbon ending in a dull dark metal star. No wax, no seals, no rings, no cords.

The five books, left to right:
1) Book 1, common: a milky-white crystal, almost no glow; valor 0 of 1 — one single faded ribbon and nothing more; padlocks: the top one open and shining, the four below closed; level 34; combat power 1240.
2) Book 2, rare: a yellow crystal and a soft yellow glow; valor 1 of 2 — two ribbons: the left one yellow with a glowing star tip, the right one faded; padlocks: the top two open and shining, the three below closed; level 150; combat power 8420.
3) Book 3, unique: a turquoise crystal and a turquoise glow; valor 2 of 3 — three ribbons: the left two turquoise with glowing star tips, the right one faded; padlocks: the top three open, the two below closed; level 350; combat power 48350.
4) Book 4, epic: a violet crystal and a violet glow; valor 3 of 4 — four ribbons: the left three violet with glowing star tips, the right one faded; padlocks: the top four open, the lowest closed; level 700; combat power 210600.
5) Book 5, timeless: a green crystal and a strong green glow; valor 5 of 5 — five ribbons, all green with glowing star tips; all five padlocks open and shining; level 1200; combat power 912780.

No words, no letters, no real-world alphabets, no Roman numerals, no runes, glyphs or markings that look like writing, no titles or lettering on covers, spines or pages, no handwriting, no lines of text, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no captions or labels. The only characters anywhere in the picture are the digits of the level and combat power numbers — no word Level, no Lv, no abbreviations such as CP, BP or PWR; the name plate stays blank. No wax seals, no seals of any kind, no cords with rings. No skulls, no skeletons, no blood. No pentagrams, no occult signs, no crosses, no religious symbols. No bright polished gold, no glossy plastic shine, no clean bright mobile-game UI look. No phone mockup, no hands, no table, no floor, no tilted books, no perspective. The hero has exactly two arms and two hands; no empty eyes.

Art style: dark fantasy game UI art for a mobile RPG — gloomy, heavy, noble and uneasy. Hand-painted digital painting: visible confident brush strokes, simplified planes, deep near-black shadows, crisp rim light on the edges. A muted, desaturated palette: soot black (#050607, #121518), graphite (#262B31), blackened iron, old dark leather, dark bronze, yellowed bone, weathered stone. Everything is matte, worn and aged: no bright polished gold, no gloss, no shiny jewellery, no clean saturated game-UI colors. Light is scarce and precious: the frame is lit from below with a crisp rim light along its edges; only its magical parts glow from within. No photorealism, no 3D-render look, no anime, no cartoon, no flat vector style.

Draw exactly one image in a single pass: no alternative versions, no text in the reply.

Format: a frame for a fighter card on the battle screen of a dark fantasy mobile card battler. Landscape 5:4 canvas, seen straight on, flat, not in perspective, perfectly symmetric from left to right. The frame is a landscape rectangle, and its window — the empty opening where the game later puts the fighter's portrait — is a clean landscape rectangle with straight inner edges and small square corners, about 1.35 times as wide as it is tall; the window takes almost the whole frame. Everything on the canvas is solid pure black except the frame itself: the window is pure black and completely empty — no face, no figure, no glow, no smoke, no mist, no reflection, no pattern inside it.

Proportions, strictly: all four bars are equally slim — the top bar is as slim as the two side bars and the bottom bar, each about 3% of the frame width; the side bars and the bottom bar are plain, with no ornament on them; nothing hangs below the bottom bar and nothing sticks out sideways from the lower two thirds of the frame. All ornament stands on the top bar and at the two top corners: it rises above the top bar by at most one tenth of the frame width; horns and spikes at the top corners grow upward and only a little outward, reaching sideways past the side bars by at most one thirtieth of the frame width. Nothing hangs down into the window: the inner edge of the frame is a clean straight line on all four sides. No smoke, sparks, motes or particles anywhere around the frame.

In the game it is seen very small, about 90 pixels wide: bold, simple, strong silhouettes and one clear accent rather than fine filigree; a thin crisp light rim runs along the inner edge of the frame so that the portrait separates from it. The enemy frames form a ladder of danger: the more dangerous the enemy, the heavier and more terrifying its frame — bone, thorns, horns, dark flame, glowing cracks of carst — awe and dread, never wealth or gloss.

The side: our heroes — one frame for every hero of the player's squad, standing against the enemy. Not a threat: dignity, age and quiet strength, like the binding of an old book of legends. A slim frame of dark leather edged with thin dark bronze lines, bound at the four corners with small blackened iron corner pieces like the corners of an old book cover; a few tiny bronze studs along the bars. At the top center a small round socket of dark bronze set into the top bar, about twice as tall as the bar, empty and pure black inside; nothing else rises above the top bar. Faint cold turquoise carst light (#48E5D4) comes from below and catches the lower corners; everything else is matte and dim. The bars are very slim, like a thin book binding.

The background is solid pure black (#000000), flat, edge to edge: no gradient, no texture, no floor, no cast shadow, no vignette, no checkerboard. Any glow stays close to the frame and fades into the black within a short distance. The whole frame with all its ornament fits inside the central 90% of the canvas: an empty black margin stays on every side — top, bottom, left and right.

No text, no letters, no numbers, no real-world alphabets, no runes or markings that look like writing, no watermark, no signature, no logo, no interface elements other than the frame itself: no buttons, no bars, no gauges, no name plate, no label, no banner with lettering. No skulls, no blood, no gore. No pentagrams, no occult signs, no crosses, no religious symbols. No bright polished gold, no glossy plastic shine. Nothing at all inside the window.

The cover works as a picture frame. In its middle there is ONE large empty rectangular window with straight edges and slightly rounded corners, running from about 12% to about 74% of the book's height and from about 12% to about 85% of its width. The window is pure flat black: nothing at all is painted in it — no portrait, no figure, no picture, no glow, no texture, no reflection, no inner border. The spine is the left edge of the book. Around the window the cover shows plain calm bands of its material: a strip along the right edge about 15% of the book's width, a band along the top about 12% of its height, and a broad band along the bottom about 26% of its height. The interface places its own badges, a gem, padlocks, a name plate and numbers on these bands, so none of those are painted: the bands carry only the cover's own material, corners and ornament.

The attached image is the approved concept sheet: five hero books stand side by side, from left to right book 1 to book 5, each with the painted portrait of an old dwarf, round badges with numbers, a crystal, padlocks and ribbons. Take from it ONLY the design of the one cover named below — its material, construction, corners, ornament, wear, colors and brushwork — and paint that cover alone, large, with the window empty. Format: a game UI piece for a dark fantasy mobile RPG — the front cover of ONE closed book that serves as a hero card, vertical 9:16, seen perfectly straight on: flat, upright, not tilted, no perspective. The book fills the canvas up to the black margin. The whole canvas is solid pure black — outside the book and inside its window alike; only the cover itself is painted.

The cover works as a picture frame. In its middle there is ONE large empty rectangular window with straight edges and slightly rounded corners, running from about 12% to about 74% of the book's height and from about 12% to about 85% of its width. The window is pure flat black: nothing at all is painted in it — no portrait, no figure, no picture, no glow, no texture, no reflection, no inner border. The spine is the left edge of the book. Around the window the cover shows plain calm bands of its material: a strip along the right edge about 15% of the book's width, a band along the top about 12% of its height, and a broad band along the bottom about 26% of its height. The interface places its own badges, a gem, padlocks, a name plate and numbers on these bands, so none of those are painted: the bands carry only the cover's own material, corners and ornament.

The attached image is the approved concept sheet: five hero books stand side by side, from left to right book 1 to book 5, each with the painted portrait of an old dwarf, round badges with numbers, a crystal, padlocks and ribbons. Take from it ONLY the design of the one cover named below — its material, construction, corners, ornament, wear, colors and brushwork — and paint that cover alone, large, with the window empty. Never copy from the sheet: the dwarf and his portrait, the round badges with numbers, the crystal at the top, the round orange element medallion, the padlocks along the right edge, the shield icon, the crossed swords and numbers, the name plate, the ribbons and stars below the books, or the colored glow around the books.

The cover to paint: BOOK 2 — the second book from the left on the sheet: a sturdier book whose dark grey-black leather cover is framed by broad bands of dark blackened iron with small rivets, four heavy iron corner pieces, and a leather tab with a round iron boss that fastens the cover at the middle of its left edge, reaching a little over the window. Solid, practical, protected.

The background is solid pure black (#000000), flat, edge to edge: no gradient, no texture, no floor, no cast shadow, no vignette, no checkerboard. Any glow stays close to the subject and fades into the black within a short distance. The whole subject with its glow fits inside the central 90% of the canvas in both width and height: an empty black margin stays on every side — top, bottom, left and right.
